findings.claim: sugar and acid both run high, so it tastes loud rather than merely sweet
findings.because: Oregon State's comparison of nine blackberry genotypes (Du, Qian lab, 2009) measured Marion at 11.1 Brix and 1.8 percent titratable acidity, and Thornless Evergreen at 13.7 Brix and 0.9 percent. Against the berry the sentence names, Marion has less sugar and twice the acid. Across the nine it sits at moderate sugar and middling acid. The 'loud' taste comes from acid and aroma (16 times Evergreen's furaneol), not from high sugar. The furaneol, linalool and beta-ionone claims check out.
findings.fix: it carries twice Evergreen's acid on less sugar, so it tastes loud rather than merely sweet

findings.claim: since water pools between the drupelets and dilutes the juice
findings.because: Dilution is not the reason to wash at the last moment. Wet fruit is the problem: water left on soft drupelets speeds gray mold (Botrytis) and leakage within hours. That is the same failure the store field warns about, and it is why the Blackberry entry keeps fruit unwashed.
findings.fix: since wet drupelets leak and mold within hours

findings.claim: a solid block melted and set again
findings.because: A clump in the bag shows the fruit got warm and refroze, or was frozen wet or slowly, but it does not prove it melted. Some frozen packs are also meant to be solid, such as sugar packs and bulk pails. Worded as proof, it tells a cook more than the bag can show.
findings.fix: a solid block has warmed and refrozen, so expect weeping

findings.claim: Cook frozen fruit from frozen.
findings.because: The entry sends most readers to frozen fruit (it says more than 95 percent of the crop is frozen, pureed or juiced), and it lists "raw" among the methods and suggests sieved pulp for sorbet. Frozen berries are picked and frozen without any heat step. They are a documented vehicle for norovirus and hepatitis A: the large European outbreaks of 2012 to 2014 were traced to frozen berries, and so were several US outbreaks. Freezing kills neither virus. The Irish and other EU food safety authorities advise bringing frozen berries to a full boil for at least one minute before they go into anything served uncooked, and that heat inactivates both. The entry gives the cook none of this, while its methods point them at smoothies, sorbet and raw garnish. The Cilantro entry already states the equivalent fact for a raw herb, so leaving it out here is inconsistent with the Lexicon.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Frozen berries are frozen raw and have carried norovirus and hepatitis A, which freezing does not kill: bring them to a full boil for a minute before they go into sorbet, fool or anything served uncooked, and cook them from frozen." This runs longer than the words it replaces because the safety fact requires it. If prep has to stay near 280 characters, cut the closing baking-soda sentence rather than this one.

findings.claim: which is why more than 95 percent of the crop is shaken off by machine in July and frozen, pureed or juiced.
findings.because: The 95 percent figure is the share that is processed (frozen, puree, juice). The machine-harvested share is lower: Oregon State University sources put it at about 70 to 90 percent. The sentence gives the processing figure to the harvest method. Softness also explains why the crop is processed, not why it is machine picked.
findings.fix: which is why most is machine shaken in July and over 95 percent frozen, pureed or juiced.

findings.claim: dull, deep black, plump, longer than round, soft enough to give under a fingertip, no red drupelets. Reject leaking punnets and any smell of wine.
findings.because: This nearly repeats the Blackberry entry's choose line: "Dull, deep black all over, plump and yielding, with no red or green drupelets left... Reject leaking fruit and any punnet smelling of fermentation." The definition already sends the reader to Blackberry, and the house rule is to agree with a sibling entry without repeating it. Only the shape, the softness and the frozen-bag test are specific to Marion.
findings.fix: Longer than round and softer than other blackberries: a ripe Marion gives under a fingertip; reject a stained, wet punnet. Frozen, shake the bag: loose berries froze fast; a solid block melted and set again.

findings.claim: released in Oregon in 1956 and named for Marion County, so
findings.because: The contract says mechanism first and no history for its own sake. Where the name comes from is trivia that delays the mechanism. The hint requires the cultivar status and the cross, not the county.
findings.fix: released in Oregon in 1956, so

findings.claim: Sieve pulp for sauce or sorbet, where the seeds show.
findings.because: The Blackberry entry already closes on "sieve the pulp if the seeds are coarse", so this repeats a sibling entry and adds nothing specific to Marion.
findings.fix: Delete the sentence, or replace it with a Marion-specific knife or handling fact of the same length or shorter.

findings.claim: milder in both sugar and acid than a raspberry
findings.because: The acid half holds: every source describes salmonberry as less tart than raspberry. The sugar half is not established. I found no published Brix figures for salmonberry, several regional guides call ripe fruit sweeter and honey-like, and UAF extension notes wide variation. The house rule says to leave out what cannot be confirmed.
findings.fix: milder and less tart than a raspberry

findings.claim: the color marks the bush, not the ripeness
findings.because: The color morph is genetic: some plants bear yellow-orange fruit and others red. But the fruit still changes color as it ripens, from green through yellow and orange. UAF extension notes that yellow, orange and red berries can all be seen on a single plant, so an orange berry on a red bush can be underripe. As written, a cook could pick salmon-colored fruit off a red bush as ripe.
findings.fix: the bush sets the shade, so match the ripest fruit on that plant

findings.claim: for jam add pectin rather than boiling it down
findings.because: The brief puts the mechanism first, but the entry never names the reason: the fruit is low in pectin. The sealed Raspberry entry says raspberry has moderate pectin and sets with lemon and a hard boil, so the reader needs to know why this relative needs added pectin. UAF extension salmonberry jam and jelly recipes all use commercial pectin.
findings.fix: for jam add pectin, since the fruit has too little to set, rather than boiling it down

findings.claim: it collapses and weeps within hours of picking
findings.because: This is only true at field or room temperature. UAF extension gives two to three days refrigerated, and the entry's own store field allows a day or two. Unqualified, the two fields read as a contradiction.
findings.fix: it collapses and weeps within hours in a warm bucket

findings.claim: "Plump, glossy and whole, in any shade from gold to ruby; the color marks the bush, not the ripeness."
findings.because: The entry itself says salmonberry is foraged far more than it is sold, so the cook holding one has usually picked it. Yet it never says which feature identifies the plant, and it tells the reader that color is no guide. In the same moist Northwest woods and stream edges, two red berries grow that can make a forager ill. Baneberry (Actaea rubra) carries glossy red berries that are highly toxic. Red elderberry (Sambucus racemosa) holds cyanogenic glycosides in the raw fruit and seeds. Both are smooth single berries borne in clusters on a stalk. The check that works is structure: an aggregate of drupelets that slips off a conical core and comes away hollow marks a Rubus. The definition does describe this structure, but it never presents it as the identification, and the one place that tells a forager what to pick (choose) invites any gold-to-red berry.
findings.fix: Plump, glossy and whole, gold to ruby; the color marks the bush, not the ripeness. A ripe one lets go of the core at a light tug and comes away hollow: that cup of drupelets is the check, never a smooth single berry in a stalked cluster like baneberry or red elderberry. Reject berries that cling, feel hard and matte, or leak juice or show mold.

findings.claim: "jam", "syrup", "sorbet"
findings.because: The contract asks for lowercase verbs or short noun forms naming what the cook does. These three name products, not methods, and none appears anywhere in the corpus methods vocabulary. The corpus uses gerunds: "preserving" 37 times, "freezing" 6, "macerating" 6. Raspberry, the sibling entry this one is modeled on, lists ["raw","macerating","preserving","baking","freezing"]. The entry's own store field recommends freezing on a tray, so "freezing" belongs in the list.
findings.fix: ["raw", "macerating", "preserving", "freezing", "baking"]

findings.claim: "built like a Raspberry" ... "than a raspberry"
findings.because: A common noun is capitalized in the middle of a sentence, and the same entry lowercases the same word three sentences later. When the corpus cross-references an entry by name, it uses a parenthetical ("see Papaya" in Pawpaw), not a capital inside running prose.
findings.fix: "built like a raspberry (see Raspberry):" or simply "built like a raspberry:"

findings.claim: "each a thin skin of juicy flesh around one hard pit"
findings.because: A drupelet is a thin skin holding juicy flesh around a pit. As written, the skin seems to be made of flesh. The next sentence also switches from "receptacle" to "core" for the same structure, so a cook reading about the separation layer cannot be sure it is the same part.
findings.fix: "each a thin skin over juicy flesh around one hard pit" and "a separation layer forms between fruit and receptacle"

findings.claim: "It is the first wild berry of the Northwest year."
findings.because: This calendar fact stands alone between the mechanism (the watery build that makes the fruit collapse) and the closing instruction, which breaks the mechanism-then-tomorrow order the contract asks for. The season field already carries the same fact. Folding it into the previous sentence keeps the fact and restores the flow, with no extra length.
findings.fix: "...within hours of picking, and why the first wild berry of the Northwest year is foraged far more than it is sold." (delete the standalone sentence)

findings.claim: They carry a cyanogenic glycoside, the compound family behind the bitter almond of an apricot kernel
findings.because: The glycoside is not the flavor. When a seed is broken, amygdalin (and prunasin) is cleaved to benzaldehyde, the almond note, plus hydrogen cyanide. Ripe saskatoons hold about 42 to 118 mg/kg amygdalin, confined to the seeds, and buds, flowers, leaves and twigs carry more than the fruit. The house rule asks for exactly this safety fact about the plant, and the entry names the compound family without saying what it releases.
findings.fix: They carry amygdalin: a broken seed yields benzaldehyde, the bitter almond of an apricot kernel, and a trace of hydrogen cyanide. The leaves and twigs hold more than the fruit.

findings.claim: cooking brings that almond note forward, so a baked saskatoon tastes faintly of marzipan
findings.because: The almond note comes from benzaldehyde, which an enzyme releases from the glycoside when seed tissue is disrupted. Heat denatures that enzyme and does not create the compound, so 'cooking brings it forward' names a mechanism nobody has shown. Cooked fruit does taste of almond, most likely because the softened seeds break open in the filling and give up benzaldehyde already formed.
findings.fix: softened seeds split in a filling, so a baked saskatoon tastes faintly of marzipan

findings.claim: makes pectin reluctant to set: lemon juice fixes both
findings.because: The fruit is low in pectin as well as low in acid. Lemon supplies the acid a gel needs, but it cannot make up for missing pectin. Saskatoon jam sets only with added pectin or a long reduction, and frozen fruit sets worse still.
findings.fix: and the fruit is itself low in pectin: lemon fixes the acid, but a jam still wants added pectin or a long reduction

findings.claim: The flesh is sugary and low in acid ... lemon juice fixes both
findings.because: 'preserving' is a listed method, and saskatoons run about pH 4.2 to 4.4, close to the 4.6 line that separates acid foods from low-acid foods in canning. Canning guidance for whole saskatoons adds bottled lemon juice: 1 tablespoon (about 15 g) per pint jar or 2 (about 30 g) per quart. The entry treats lemon only as seasoning and never states the pH.
findings.fix: The flesh runs near pH 4.3, close to the canning line, so canned fruit takes bottled lemon juice, about 15 grams per pint jar; lemon also lifts a flat filling.

findings.claim: The color is anthocyanin, which turns green gray in an alkaline batter, so keep baking soda modest.
findings.because: The existing Blueberry entry already explains anthocyanin, its green-gray shift in alkali and the soda-heavy muffin batter. The brief says not to repeat existing content and to cross-reference by name instead.
findings.fix: The pigment behaves exactly as in Blueberry, so keep baking soda modest.

findings.claim: Amelanchier, sold as saskatoon, juneberry or shadbush
findings.because: This reads as if the three are one fruit. Saskatoon is Amelanchier alnifolia, the western and prairie species that most cultivated fruit comes from. Juneberry and shadbush usually mean eastern species such as A. canadensis, A. arborea and A. laevis, whose fruit is often smaller and varies more in flavor.
findings.fix: Amelanchier: the saskatoon is A. alnifolia, and juneberry or shadbush usually an eastern cousin,

findings.claim: Reject split, leaking or moldy berries
findings.because: The definition opens by saying the fruit is a pome and not a berry. Calling it 'berries' three fields later undoes that point for the reader.
findings.fix: Reject split, leaking or moldy fruit

findings.claim: The flesh is sugary and low in acid, which makes a cooked filling taste flat and makes pectin reluctant to set: lemon juice fixes both.
findings.because: 'preserving' is one of the listed methods, and for a preserve the acid matters for safety as well as taste. Saskatoon pH runs about 4.2 to 4.4, only just under the 4.6 line for water-bath canning, and wild fruit varies. That is why published saskatoon jam and pie-filling recipes add lemon juice. As written, the entry treats lemon as seasoning, so a cook could taste a jar and decide to leave it out.
findings.fix: The flesh is sugary and low in acid, near pH 4.3, just under the 4.6 line for water-bath canning: lemon juice brightens a filling, helps pectin set, and in a jar is part of the acid, not seasoning.

findings.claim: Red-orange flat clusters belong to another tree, such as mountain ash.
findings.because: This sentence carries the plate correction, but mountain ash is not the dangerous mix-up. A dark blue-black berry ripening in the same months and habitats is the real risk: common buckthorn (Rhamnus cathartica, a strong purgative that has invaded the Midwest and Northeast, where two of the plates place this fruit), moonseed, pokeweed and Virginia creeper. The check that tells them apart is the serviceberry's five-pointed dried crown at the blossom end plus several small soft seeds inside. Buckthorn has no crown, three or four hard seeds, and fruit packed tight at the leaf bases. A forager matching on color alone gets the wrong shrub. The matsutake precedent in the contract allows the extra length.
findings.fix: Red-orange flat clusters are mountain ash, not this. Every berry needs a five-pointed crown at the blossom end and several soft seeds: blue-black fruit with no crown and three or four hard seeds, packed at the leaf bases, is buckthorn, a purgative.

findings.claim: Pick off stems and leaves, rinse only just before use, and dry on a towel.
findings.because: The cook is not told why this matters. Prunasin runs higher in the leaves, buds and flowers than in the ripe fruit, and underripe red fruit carries more cyanogenic glycoside than purple fruit. Serviceberry foliage has poisoned grazing livestock. Without the reason, a cook may leave stems in a bulk batch or steep the leaves as a tea.
findings.fix: Pick off every stem and leaf, which carry more of the cyanogenic glycoside than the fruit, then rinse only just before use and dry on a towel.

findings.claim: They carry a cyanogenic glycoside, the compound family behind the bitter almond of an apricot kernel, and cooking brings that almond note forward
findings.because: The toxin is introduced only as a flavor, and the sentence can be read as saying heat increases the compound. The ripe fruit holds amygdalin at about 42 to 118 mg/kg and prunasin at about 5 to 17 mg/kg, almost all of it in the seeds. Heat and ripening break these glycosides down; they do not concentrate them. The Apricot exemplar states the kernel fact plainly ('use it as a flavoring, not food'), and this entry should be just as plain.
findings.fix: They carry amygdalin and prunasin, the cyanogenic glycosides of an apricot kernel, in small amounts that fall as the fruit ripens and as it cooks, and baking softens the seeds until that almond note comes through

findings.claim: "The flesh is sugary and low in acid, which makes a cooked filling taste flat and makes pectin reluctant to set: lemon juice fixes both."
findings.because: Two problems. First, the entry lists "preserving" but leaves out the safety fact behind it. Saskatoon pH runs about 4.2 to 4.4, just under the 4.6 limit for water-bath canning, which is why tested canning recipes add lemon juice. Second, the fruit is also low in pectin. Lemon lowers the pH and helps a set, but many jams still need added pectin or a long reduction. "Fixes both" overstates it and disagrees with the Huckleberry entry ("Pectin is low, so a jam needs added pectin or a long reduction").
findings.fix: "The flesh is sugary and low in acid, near pH 4.4, which makes a filling taste flat and sits just under the 4.6 line for water-bath canning; pectin is low too. Lemon goes into every filling and every jar, and a jam wants a long boil or added pectin."

findings.claim: "Pick off stems and leaves, rinse only just before use, and dry on a towel."
findings.because: The definition names the cyanogenic glycoside but places it only in the seeds. Amelanchier leaves and stems carry more of it than the fruit does. Prep gives the instruction without that reason, so a cook steeping whole clusters for a syrup or juice has no cause to follow it. The contract says prep is "the part people get wrong". The current field is 273 characters, so the replacement has to be tighter to fit the 280 limit.
findings.fix: Whole field: "Pick off stems and leaves, which hold more glycoside than the fruit; rinse just before use and towel dry. Nothing to pit: the soft seeds stay in and the dried blossom crown is edible. For a pie, toss 600 grams of fruit with 30 grams of lemon juice and the sugar."

findings.claim: "The color is anthocyanin, which turns green gray in an alkaline batter, so keep baking soda modest."
findings.because: This repeats the Blueberry entry, which already explains that anthocyanin turns "blue then green-gray in alkali" and rings a soda-heavy muffin teal. The brief says to cross-reference a sibling entry and never repeat its content. "green gray" also breaks the corpus spelling, which is "green-gray" in both Blueberry and Huckleberry.
findings.fix: "Its anthocyanin answers to pH as in Blueberry, so keep baking soda modest."

findings.claim: "Reject split, leaking or moldy berries: one wet one spoils the basket."
findings.because: The definition opens by saying the fruit "is a pome and not a berry". Calling them berries two fields later contradicts the entry's own first fact.
findings.fix: "Reject split, leaking or moldy fruit: one wet one spoils the basket."

findings.claim: In this batch Loquat says 'never grind, crush or steep' the seeds, Hawthorn says never grind or blend them, and the existing Crabapple and Quince say the same. Serviceberry describes the same amygdalin chemistry at greater length and then says 'Nothing to pit: the soft seeds stay in', with the seeds 'softened and split' in a baked fruit. A cook reading the pomes together sees a contradiction and no reason for it.
findings.because: In this batch Loquat says 'never grind, crush or steep' the seeds, Hawthorn says never grind or blend them, and the existing Crabapple and Quince say the same. Serviceberry describes the same amygdalin chemistry at greater length and then says 'Nothing to pit: the soft seeds stay in', with the seeds 'softened and split' in a baked fruit. A cook reading the pomes together sees a contradiction and no reason for it.
findings.fix: Add half a sentence giving the reason, stated as a fact about the plant: the seeds are small and few, and each carries only a trace, which is why they stay in the way apple pips do in a whole apple. To make room, trim the benzaldehyde and apricot-kernel aside to one clause.

findings.claim: Pectin and acid together are why haws set a firm jelly with no added pectin.
findings.because: The entry itself says C. monogyna haws are 'only mildly tart raw', and that is right: hedgerow haws are low in acid. Standard haw jelly recipes (River Cottage style, Practical Self Reliance, Farmersgirl Kitchen) add lemon juice, around 1/4 cup per 2 cups of juice, because the fruit's own acid is not enough to set its pectin. Pectin alone explains why no commercial pectin is needed. The acid is added.
findings.fix: Pectin sets haw jelly with none added; hedgerow haws need lemon for acid.

findings.claim: kin to apple, quince and medlar, built the other way round:
findings.because: Medlar (Mespilus germanica) is built exactly like hawthorn, with thin flesh around five bony pyrenes. It is the sister genus to Crataegus, some botanists sink it into Crataegus as C. germanica, and the two hybridize (x Crataemespilus). As written, the sentence says medlar is built like an apple.
findings.fix: kin to apple and quince but built, like medlar, the other way round:

findings.claim: Simmer them whole in water until the skins split, pass them through a food mill, and sweeten the pulp;
findings.because: The skins split early, while the mealy flesh is still firm. Haws need roughly 40 to 60 minutes of simmering with mashing before they give up juice and pectin. The sentence also gives the food mill as the route to the jelly it just described, but jelly comes from liquor dripped through a jelly bag. Milled pulp makes a cloudy jelly and is the base for haw cheese, ketchup or leather.
findings.fix: Simmer them whole until soft, about 45 minutes; drip the liquor for jelly, or food-mill it for pulp;

findings.claim: Forage only a tree you know as hawthorn by its thorns and lobed leaves; cotoneaster fruit looks similar.
findings.because: Cotoneaster has no thorns, so it is the easy look-alike to rule out. The one a forager can actually mistake for hawthorn is firethorn (Pyracantha): it is thorny, carries clusters of red to orange pomes, and has cyanogenic seeds, but its leaves are unlobed and evergreen. Naming cotoneaster alone suggests that thorns settle the ID, when it is the lobed leaves that separate hawthorn from firethorn.
findings.fix: Forage only a tree with both thorns and lobed leaves: firethorn is thorny but unlobed, and cotoneaster has no thorns.

findings.claim: Deep red, firm and glossy
findings.because: Ripe color depends on the species. The plate is 'Northwest Fruits', and the hawthorn native to the Pacific Northwest, C. douglasii (black hawthorn), ripens purple-black. A cook there would read 'deep red' as the only ripe color. The red haws in that region are the introduced C. monogyna.
findings.fix: Deep red (black on black hawthorn), firm and glossy

findings.claim: Forage only a tree you know as hawthorn by its thorns and lobed leaves; cotoneaster fruit looks similar.
findings.because: The look-alike that actually sits beside hawthorn in hedges and car parks is firethorn (Pyracantha), which has thorns too. What tells it apart is its small, glossy, evergreen leaves, which are toothed but never lobed, so the check has to say that thorns alone are not enough. The entry also never says why cotoneaster matters: its fruit carries cyanogenic glycosides and is mildly poisonous. That is the fact that turns a similar-looking berry into a hazard. As written, a forager who finds thorns and red pomes on a pyracantha has passed half the test.
findings.fix: Forage only a deciduous tree with long single thorns and lobed leaves: thorns alone are not enough, since firethorn has them on small unlobed evergreen leaves. Cotoneaster, thornless, has similar red fruit that is mildly poisonous.

findings.claim: Dried shanzha slices keep a year sealed and dark.
findings.because: Dried shanzha is usually the whole fruit sliced across, so many slices still hold cut pieces of the amygdalin-bearing stones. The definition and prep tell the cook to keep the stones whole and out of the pot. The one product where they arrive already cut open gets no warning, so a cook grinding or blending slices for a powder or sauce would break the entry's own rule without knowing it.
findings.fix: Dried shanzha slices keep a year sealed and dark; many still hold cut stone pieces, so pick those out before blending or grinding, or steep and strain.

findings.claim: Chinese shanzha, Crataegus pinnatifida, runs to 2.5 cm, is properly sour, and is the fruit behind haw flakes and tanghulu.
findings.because: Hawthorn fruit is also a heart herb. Its concentrated preparations, meaning strong decoctions of the dried slices and extracts, are documented to add to the effect of digoxin and of blood pressure and nitrate drugs. A cook serving hawthorn tea or a concentrate needs that fact about the plant. The evidence comes from concentrated forms, not from jelly or a candied skewer, so it should be stated as a fact about the fruit, with no verdict about any dish or any diner.
findings.fix: Add after the shanzha sentence: "Concentrated hawthorn, as strong tea or extract, can add to the action of digoxin and blood pressure drugs." Trim elsewhere to stay inside 1200 characters.

findings.claim: "Pectin and acid together are why haws set a firm jelly with no added pectin. Simmer them whole in water until the skins split, pass them through a food mill, and sweeten the pulp;"
findings.because: Only the pectin half is right. The entry says itself that hedgerow haws are "only mildly tart raw". The fruit is short of acid, which is why standard haw jelly recipes add lemon juice for a set. The closing instruction also gives the wrong product: food-milled, sweetened pulp makes haw cheese or paste, not jelly. Jelly is juice dripped through a jelly bag. A cook who follows this sentence tomorrow and wants jelly gets a soft, cloudy set.
findings.fix: "Haws carry ample pectin but hedgerow fruit is short of acid, so jelly takes lemon and no added pectin. Simmer them whole until the skins split, drip the juice through a jelly bag;" (179 characters, the same length as the text it replaces; the tanghulu clause after the semicolon stays)

findings.claim: "Forage only a tree you know as hawthorn by its thorns and lobed leaves; cotoneaster fruit looks similar."
findings.because: This names a look-alike but not why it matters, and it leaves out the one that thorns do not exclude. Cotoneaster is thornless. Firethorn (Pyracantha) has thorns and red pome fruit in the same clusters, and leaf shape is what tells it apart: its leaves are unlobed. Both fruits are mildly toxic raw. The house rule asks for the look-alike stated as a fact about the plant, and here that fact is missing.
findings.fix: Whole field, 274 characters: "Deep red, firm and glossy, stalks on, in heavy clusters; shanzha large, bright red and freckled pale. Reject shriveled, split or brown fruit. Forage only a thorny tree with lobed leaves: cotoneaster is thornless, firethorn has unlobed leaves, and both upset the stomach raw."

findings.claim: "and they freeze well for jelly, since cooking undoes any softening."
findings.because: Cooking does not undo softening. Freezing ruptures the cells and the fruit stays soft. That doesn't matter for jelly, because the fruit is simmered and strained, so its texture is never needed. The reason the sentence gives is a false mechanism.
findings.fix: "and they freeze well for jelly, which never needs their texture."

findings.claim: The amygdalin instruction appears three times inside the entry: the definition says the stones 'are strained out and never ground', store says 'pick them out before grinding or blending', and prep says 'never put them in a blender'. Together they repeat almost word for word the existing Crabapple sentence ('the jelly bag strains them out... a butter goes through a food mill, never a blender'). The definition also says the fruit is rich in pectin twice ('rich in pectin' and 'Haws carry ample pectin').
findings.because: The amygdalin instruction appears three times inside the entry: the definition says the stones 'are strained out and never ground', store says 'pick them out before grinding or blending', and prep says 'never put them in a blender'. Together they repeat almost word for word the existing Crabapple sentence ('the jelly bag strains them out... a butter goes through a food mill, never a blender'). The definition also says the fruit is rich in pectin twice ('rich in pectin' and 'Haws carry ample pectin').
findings.fix: Cut the amygdalin sentence from the definition. State it once in prep: 'The stones carry amygdalin, as crabapple pips do: let the food mill or jelly bag hold them back, never a blender.' Keep the dried-shanzha note in store because it is new. Make the second pectin mention only about acid: 'hedgerow fruit is short of acid, so jelly takes lemon and needs no added pectin'.

findings.claim: That fragility, not flavor, is why it is so rarely sold fresh: it has no starch to turn into sugar after picking, so it must come off fully ripe, and ripe it lasts two days.
findings.because: After the colon the sentence explains the missing starch, not the fragility, so the reason given does not match the claim. Starch is the reason the fruit has to be picked ripe. Picked ripe, the thin-skinned drupelets leak and rot within days, and that is why it rarely travels fresh (Wikipedia: mature fruit leaks juice easily and decays within a few days). 'No starch' is also too absolute. Brambles carry almost no starch, which is how the Apricot and Raspberry entries put it ('almost no starch reserve', 'with no starch it gains no sugar' after picking). Boysenberry parentage (dewberry x loganberry per USDA Corvallis, with raspberry and blackberry behind them) and the late-1920s California origin both check out.
findings.fix: That fragility, not flavor, keeps it out of shops: with almost no starch to turn into sugar, it must be picked fully ripe, and ripe it lasts two days.

findings.claim: Rinse only just before use, in a bowl of cold water rather than under the tap, then lift them onto a towel.
findings.because: The definition calls the drupelets thinner skinned and fuller of juice than a blackberry's, so the fruit tears and leaks under its own weight. Soaking such fruit lets it take on water and bleed juice. The sibling entries agree: Raspberry says 'Do not wash unless you must: they take on water and slump', and Blackberry says 'Shop fruit needs nothing'. Making a rinse the routine step contradicts the entry's own mechanism and its siblings.
findings.fix: Wash only if you must, just before use: a brief dip in a bowl of cold water, never the tap, then lift onto a towel.

findings.claim: To keep them, open-freeze on a tray, then bag: they hold about a year at -18C (0F), for pie and jam, never for garnish.
findings.because: The entry itself says boysenberries are mostly bought frozen. Frozen berries are among the best documented carriers of hepatitis A and norovirus: the EU mixed-berry hepatitis A outbreak of 2013, the repeated Nordic norovirus outbreaks from frozen raspberries, and several US and Australian frozen-berry recalls. Freezing does not inactivate either virus. Food safety agencies such as FSAI advise boiling imported frozen berries for one minute before eating them. The only reason the entry gives for 'never for garnish' is texture, so a cook reads it as advice about looks and will still put frozen berries raw into smoothies, fools or a coulis. This is the safety fact a cook needs about this product, and it is missing.
findings.fix: Refrigerate unwashed at 0 to 2C (32 to 36F), one layer deep on paper, and use within two days; gray mold spreads berry to berry on contact. Open-freeze on a tray, then bag: they hold about a year at -18C (0F). Frozen berries have carried hepatitis A and norovirus, which freezing does not kill, so bring them to a boil in pie, sauce or jam rather than serve them raw.

findings.claim: Rinse only just before use, in a bowl of cold water rather than under the tap, then lift them onto a towel.
findings.because: Food safety guidance, the FDA's for example, is to rinse produce under running water and not to soak it in standing water. A shared bowl moves microbes and mold spores from one berry to all the others, and for a fruit the entry already says carries spreading gray mold, the bowl is the wrong advice. A gentle stream through a colander protects the fragile drupelets just as well.
findings.fix: Rinse only just before use, in a colander under a gentle stream of cold water, then spread them on a towel.

findings.claim: A bramble hybrid bred in California in the 1920s, with blackberry, raspberry and loganberry in its parentage, and it cooks like a blackberry with a raspberry's perfume. Like the Blackberry it leaves the cane with its soft core inside, but the drupelets are larger, thinner skinned and fuller of juice, so the fruit tears and leaks under its own weight.
findings.because: The contract says MECHANISM FIRST and no history for its own sake. This entry opens on a breeding date and a pedigree, and the mechanism (the large, thin-skinned, juicy drupelets on a soft core that tear under their own weight) only arrives in the second sentence. All three exemplars open on the working fact: Apple on malic acid and pectin, Apricot on its missing starch reserve, Asian Pear on the species and then the ripening behavior. The facts are right: the plate correction puts the boysenberry's home in California, and the parentage is sound. Only the order is wrong.
findings.fix: Its drupelets are larger, thinner skinned and juicier than a blackberry's, and like the Blackberry it leaves the cane with its soft core inside, so the fruit tears and leaks under its own weight. A 1920s California cross of blackberry, raspberry and loganberry, it cooks like a blackberry with a raspberry's perfume.

findings.claim: That fragility, not flavor, is why it is so rarely sold fresh: it has no starch to turn into sugar after picking, so it must come off fully ripe, and ripe it lasts two days.
findings.because: The colon promises to explain the fragility, but what follows is a different fact: the fruit is non-climacteric (no starch, so no sweetening after picking). Fragility and non-climacteric ripening are two separate causes, and together they are the reason it rarely ships. As written, a cook reads a non sequitur.
findings.fix: It has no starch to turn into sugar after picking, so it must come off fully ripe, and ripe it lasts two days: that fragility, not flavor, is why it is so rarely sold fresh.

findings.claim: The definition repeats two paragraphs the corpus already carries. (1) The close, 'Freezing ruptures the cells, so frozen berries slump into juice as they warm. Bake them straight from the freezer with an extra spoon of starch', is the same move as Marionberry's close in this batch ('Freezing ruptures those cells... with a little more starch than fresh fruit needs') and as the existing Huckleberry ('Ice tears the cells, so frozen fruit bleeds...'). (2) The cyanidin, pH and baking-soda sentence repeats Blueberry, Huckleberry and Black Raspberry in this batch. Read together, three cane berries end on the same frozen-pie paragraph.

Leave the frozen-pie instruction to Marionberry, where more than 95 percent of the crop is frozen.

findings.claim: The hepatitis A and norovirus fact for frozen berries is in Boysenberry's store field but in Marionberry's prep field, worded differently and with a different instruction ('boil them a minute in sauce, jam or a bubbling pie' against 'bring them to a full boil for a minute before... anything served uncooked, and cook them from frozen'). A safety fact that belongs to both siblings should sit in the same field with the same instruction.

A safety fact that belongs to both siblings should sit in the same field with the same instruction.
findings.fix: Move the sentence from store to prep so it matches Marionberry, and use Marionberry's wording: a full one-minute boil before the berries go into anything served uncooked. Keep store about storage only.

findings.claim: frozen fruit bakes and sieves as well as fresh
findings.because: Frozen Rubus fruit loses its cell structure. As it softens it leaks juice, and black raspberry juice carries four to eleven times the anthocyanin of red raspberry. Frozen fruit that sits before it goes into a batter streaks the crumb and makes it wet. In a soda-leavened batter, that loose pigment is what turns the dull blue green that the definition itself warns about. Frozen fruit really does sieve as well as fresh. It does not bake as well unless it goes into the oven still frozen.
findings.fix: frozen fruit sieves as well as fresh and bakes well straight from the freezer.

findings.claim: slipping off the stem at a touch
findings.because: When a ripe black raspberry is picked, it separates from its receptacle, the white core. It does not separate from the stem. The definition uses exactly that distinction to tell this fruit from a blackberry, so 'stem' in choose blurs the test the entry is teaching. Fruit already in a carton has no stem to slip off, so the test only applies when picking.
findings.fix: slipping off its white core at a touch and hollow inside.

findings.claim: Reject juice on the carton floor, mold, and berries with a solid core: those are blackberries.
findings.because: Blackcaps are mostly a wild, picked-yourself fruit in the Midwest (the hint says so, and prep assumes wild fruit), but the entry never says how to tell the plant apart from its dangerous neighbors. The only check it gives is hollow versus solid core, and that only separates two edible brambles. In the same woods and fencerows, pokeweed (Phytolacca americana) and the black-fruited nightshades carry glossy purple-black berries that are poisonous. The check that works: a real black raspberry is a cluster of small drupelets, picked off a thorny arching cane with a whitish bloom that rubs off. A smooth, single, glossy berry is never this plant. The Blackberry entry already gives this kind of warning for its own fruit, so this entry can point to it instead of repeating it.
findings.fix: Keep the existing three sentences and add one: "Picking wild, take only hollow caps of drupelets off a thorny cane with a white bloom; a smooth, glossy single berry, such as pokeweed or nightshade, is poisonous (see Blackberry)." The field goes to about 470 characters. That is over the 280 aim but under the 700 ceiling, and the contract allows the extra length for a look-alike warning.

findings.claim: Pick over on a tray rather than washing; if wild fruit must be rinsed, dip it briefly in a bowl of cold water and drain on paper.
findings.because: The wording treats rinsing wild fruit as a last resort. Wild fruit has been exposed to birds, deer, insects, soil splash and sometimes roadside spray, and the entry lists it for raw service. Raspberries are also a known carrier of Cyclospora and norovirus. The sister Blackberry entry says to rinse foraged fruit as the default. Commercial kitchen rules also require raw fruit to be washed before it is served ready to eat. "Store unwashed" is correct. Skipping the wash at the point of use is the mistake.
findings.fix: "Pick over on a tray. Rinse wild fruit just before use: dip it briefly in a bowl of cold water and drain on paper." (113 characters in place of 129; the sieve and staining sentences stay as they are.)

findings.claim: "like the Raspberry it leaves its white receptacle on the cane ... where a Blackberry carries its solid core with it"
findings.because: The corpus never capitalizes a common fruit name mid-sentence when it points to another entry (Huckleberry writes "blueberry's own genus", "where a blueberry is pale inside"). This definition also lowercases "red raspberry" three times further on, so the capitals are inconsistent within the entry itself. Only a proper term like "The Three Heats" takes a capital.
findings.fix: like the raspberry it leaves its white receptacle on the cane, so the fruit comes away as a hollow thimble, where a blackberry carries its solid core with it

findings.claim: "they weep and mold fast, and one soft berry spreads it to its neighbors" ... "Refrigerate unwashed in a shallow single layer"
findings.because: "Mold" is used here as a verb, so "it" has no noun to refer to. The field also leaves out the temperature that the exemplars and the sibling Huckleberry entry give for the same kind of fruit, although the contract asks for where, how long and what kills it. The house form is "0 to 2 C (32 to 36 F)", with no degree sign.
findings.fix: Refrigerate unwashed at 0 to 2 C (32 to 36 F) in a shallow single layer, one to two days at most; mold spreads berry to berry, so lift out soft ones. For longer, open-freeze on a lined tray, then bag: frozen fruit slumps but keeps its flavor. (242 characters, shorter than the original 261; this one sentence also covers the next finding.)

findings.claim: "frozen fruit bakes and sieves as well as fresh"
findings.because: Freezing ruptures the cells, so frozen berries collapse and give off more juice in a bake than fresh ones. The related Blackberry entry says of the same treatment that "the texture goes but the flavor holds", and Huckleberry says frozen fruit bleeds. The claim overstates the case and disagrees with both.
findings.fix: frozen fruit slumps but keeps its flavor (already folded into the store rewrite above)

findings.claim: "slipping off the stem at a touch and hollow inside"
findings.because: A picked black raspberry has no stem. What it slips off on the cane is the receptacle (the core), so the test only works while picking and the words name the wrong part. "Hollow inside" repeats the closing line about the solid core. The field is at 279 characters, one short of the 280 limit, so the fix has to be shorter.
findings.fix: Dull black all over, plump and dry; on the cane a ripe one slips off its core at a touch. A red or purple drupelet means underripe fruit that will not sweeten off the cane. Reject juice on the carton floor, mold, and berries with a solid core: those are blackberries. (267 characters)

findings.claim: (1) 'anthocyanins read pH: crimson in acid, violet toward neutral, a dull blue green in a batter carrying too much baking soda' is the same pH paragraph as Blueberry, Huckleberry and Boysenberry. Its own fact, cyanidin rutinosides at many times a red raspberry's level, is enough on its own. (2) choose says 'a smooth, glossy single berry belongs to a poisonous plant such as pokeweed or nightshade (see Blackberry)', but the Blackberry entry names nightshade, privet and buckthorn and never pokeweed. Pokeweed is covered in Huckleberry and Elderberry. (3) Most of the black raspberry crop is sold frozen, yet the frozen-berry hepatitis A and norovirus fact that Marionberry and Boysenberry carry is missing, and prep warms the fruit and sieves it for sauce without boiling it.
findings.because: (1) 'anthocyanins read pH: crimson in acid, violet toward neutral, a dull blue green in a batter carrying too much baking soda' is the same pH paragraph as Blueberry, Huckleberry and Boysenberry. Its own fact, cyanidin rutinosides at many times a red raspberry's level, is enough on its own. (2) choose says 'a smooth, glossy single berry belongs to a poisonous plant such as pokeweed or nightshade (see Blackberry)', but the Blackberry entry names nightshade, privet and buckthorn and never pokeweed. Pokeweed is covered in Huckleberry and Elderberry. (3) Most of the black raspberry crop is sold frozen, yet the frozen-berry hepatitis A and norovirus fact that Marionberry and Boysenberry carry is missing, and prep warms the fruit and sieves it for sauce without boiling it.
findings.fix: Keep the pigment-level fact and replace the pH clause with 'and like Blueberry it turns blue-green against baking soda'. Change the cross-reference to '(see Blackberry and Elderberry)', or drop pokeweed. In prep, add the same one-minute-boil sentence Marionberry uses for bought frozen fruit going into anything served uncooked.

findings.claim: To cook, split pulp from hull: pulp for jelly and juice, hulls for hull pie.
findings.because: In muscadines the anthocyanins, most of the polyphenolics and much of the aroma sit in the hull. Juice is made by crushing whole berries and pressing them hot, at about 70 C, to pull color from the skins. Jelly is cooked from crushed whole fruit and then strained. Pulp cooked alone gives a purple type's juice or jelly that is pale and thin in flavor. Separating pulp from hull is the hull-pie method, not the jelly or juice method.
findings.fix: To cook, crush whole berries and heat them for juice and jelly, since the hull holds the color; split pulp from hull for hull pie.

findings.claim: rich in ellagic acid, the same compound that settles out of muscadine juice as a gritty sediment on standing
findings.because: The work on muscadine juice sediment (Lee and Talcott, J. Agric. Food Chem. 2002) found free ellagic acid made up no more than about 12 percent of the sediment by weight. The rest was conjugated ellagic acid, ellagitannins and unidentified material. Calling the sediment 'the same compound' overstates it.
findings.fix: rich in ellagic acid and ellagitannins, which settle out of muscadine juice as a gritty sediment on standing

findings.claim: berries borne a few to a loose cluster
findings.because: Muscadines grow in small, loose clusters of about 3 to 40 berries, depending on the cultivar. 'A few' understates the modern cultivars.
findings.fix: berries borne in small loose clusters

findings.claim: Inside is a slipskin gel
findings.because: 'Slipskin' describes the skin, which slips off the pulp. It does not describe the gel. As written, the gel is the thing that slips.
findings.fix: Inside, a gel pulp that slips free of the hull holds

findings.claim: Simmer the pulp until the seeds float free
findings.because: Mature grape seeds are denser than the pulp and water, so they sink. They do not float. Heat loosens the gel from the seeds, and the cook watches for that.
findings.fix: Simmer the pulp until the seeds come loose

findings.claim: bronze turned golden or black gone deep purple ... Reject ... bronze ones still green
findings.because: Dark types turn from green through red to purple-black, so 'black gone deep purple' reverses the order. Many ripe bronze cultivars stay greenish-bronze with russet, so color alone can make a cook reject ripe fruit. Ripeness shows as slight give, aroma, and a berry that parts easily at the stem.
findings.fix: Full color for the type, bronze gone golden or dark types gone purple-black, with slight give and fragrant from a foot away. Check the stem scar: dry and closed keeps, torn and wet molds within days. Reject split, shriveled, sticky or rock-hard fruit.

findings.claim: The entry never mentions a look-alike. The choose field ends at "Reject split, shriveled or sticky fruit and bronze ones still green." and the definition only says "as many as five hard seeds".
findings.because: A lot of muscadines are picked off wild vines in the Southeast, and this atlas is for the cook holding the fruit. Common moonseed (Menispermum canadense) grows through the upper part of the muscadine's range, from Virginia and Tennessee down to Georgia and Alabama. Its blue-black berries hang in grape-like clusters and are toxic, and there are reported deaths from people mistaking it for wild grapes. Counting seeds is not a safe check, because a small wild muscadine can hold only one or two. The seed's shape is the check that works: every Vitis seed is a plump teardrop with a short beak, and a moonseed berry holds one flat seed shaped like a crescent or ring. The vine confirms it. Moonseed twines with no tendrils and has smooth-edged leaves, while a muscadine has unbranched tendrils and round, coarsely toothed leaves. The entry's line on seed count could even reassure a forager who is holding the wrong fruit.
findings.fix: Add to the end of choose (about 420 characters in total, under the 700 ceiling): "Picked wild, split one first and judge the seed's shape, not the count: grape seeds are plump teardrops, while moonseed, a toxic look-alike vine with smooth-edged leaves and no tendrils, carries one flat crescent-shaped seed."

findings.claim: "bronze turned golden or black gone deep purple"
findings.because: Dark muscadines ripen from green through red and purple to black, so purple is a stage they pass through before they are ripe, not the finish. As written, a cook would accept fruit that still has a purple or red cast, which is underripe and sour.
findings.fix: "bronze turned golden or dark ones gone fully black"

findings.claim: "built differently from the table grape: 40 chromosomes to vinifera's 38, and berries borne a few to a loose cluster that ripen one at a time"
findings.because: The chromosome count is botanical trivia that changes nothing a cook does, and it sits in the opening slot the contract saves for the mechanism. It also leaves the relative clause "cluster that ripen" reading as if the cluster ripens. The mechanism that matters, berries that ripen one at a time and drop, is already in the sentence.
findings.fix: "built differently from the table grape: its berries grow a few to a loose cluster, ripen one at a time"

findings.claim: "jelly"
findings.because: Every other method is a technique (raw, preserving, juicing, baking, stewing), as in the exemplars. "Jelly" names a product, and "preserving" already covers it. The hint names sweet wine as a main use, and nothing on the list covers it.
findings.fix: Replace "jelly" with "fermenting"

findings.claim: The existing Table Grape entry says to quarter grapes lengthwise for children under five because a whole grape can block a small airway. Muscadines are larger than table grapes, and the gel pulp that 'pops out' when you squeeze the stem scar to your lips is exactly that hazard, yet the entry does not mention it. A sibling needs this safety fact.
findings.because: The existing Table Grape entry says to quarter grapes lengthwise for children under five because a whole grape can block a small airway. Muscadines are larger than table grapes, and the gel pulp that 'pops out' when you squeeze the stem scar to your lips is exactly that hazard, yet the entry does not mention it. A sibling needs this safety fact.
findings.fix: Add one line to prep (or choose): 'For a child under five, never offer the squeezed-out pulp whole: the slippery, grape-sized gel is the right size and shape to block a small airway; split it and take out the seeds.'

findings.claim: The large glossy seeds, usually two to four, fill much of the fruit
findings.because: Morton (Fruits of Warm Climates, Purdue NewCrop) gives 1 to 10 seeds per loquat, "ordinarily, only 3 to 5". Two to four understates the usual count, and the hint's figure is the source of the error.
findings.fix: The large glossy seeds, usually three to five, fill much of the fruit

findings.claim: Ripe loquats hold a day on the counter and three to five days refrigerated at about 4 C (40 F)
findings.because: Both figures are too short. Postharvest studies give about 3 days of shelf life at 20 C even after cold storage, and Morton gives about 10 days at ordinary temperature. Sound fruit keeps weeks at 0 to 5 C (40 days at 0 C in trials). A home cook's ripe fruit keeps about a week in the refrigerator, and some cultivars develop chilling injury at 0 C over long storage (internal browning, dry leathery flesh).
findings.fix: Ripe loquats hold two or three days on the counter and about a week refrigerated at 2 to 4 C (36 to 40 F)

findings.claim: ripens in spring, weeks ahead of any stone fruit
findings.because: The seasons overlap. California loquats ripen mostly in April, and the first California cherries arrive in late April. Spanish nísperos (April to June) share their season with Jerte cherries. Florida fruit from February is the only crop clearly ahead. As an absolute claim, "any stone fruit" is false.
findings.fix: ripens in spring, one of the first tree fruits of the year

findings.claim: It does not ripen off the tree: the sugar is set at picking
findings.because: Loquat is classed as non-climacteric, and sugar does not rise after harvest. The postharvest literature (Foods 2023 review) notes that some cultivars ripen in a climacteric-like pattern. After picking, acid falls and color deepens a little, but the fruit does not sweeten. The claim is broadly right, but "does not ripen" overstates it; what matters to the cook is that it will not sweeten.
findings.fix: It will not sweeten off the tree: the sugar is set at picking

findings.claim: Discard the seeds whole.
findings.because: Loquat seeds release hydrogen cyanide only once they are broken, and that is exactly how people handle them. Italian nespolino liqueur and some home extract recipes crush the kernels and steep them, some jam recipes simmer the seeds in with the fruit, and loquat seed powder sold as a health food has caused cyanide poisoning (Hong Kong has issued a warning about it). The entry says to discard the seeds but never says not to grind, crush or steep them, and that is the step that actually protects someone. The 34 characters this adds are paid for by cutting 'with your fingers', so prep stays at 268 characters, inside the 280 target.
findings.fix: Pull the stem and slip the skin off from that end; ripe fruit peels like a blanched tomato. Halve, lift out the seeds and the papery membrane that lines their cavity, and drop the halves into water with lemon. Discard the seeds whole: never grind, crush or steep them.

findings.claim: hold amygdalin, which releases hydrogen cyanide when crushed.
findings.because: The fact is right but the mechanism is only half stated. The seed carries its own enzyme, which reaches the amygdalin as soon as the seed is broken. So chewing counts as much as crushing, and that is how a child or a guest who bites into a seed gets a dose. Stating the enzyme follows the house rule to explain the mechanism first, and it tells the cook why an intact seed matters.
findings.fix: hold amygdalin, which the seed's own enzyme turns into hydrogen cyanide once it is crushed or chewed.

findings.claim: Eat the soft ones raw the day you get them, and put the firm ones up as jam or poached halves.
findings.because: Nothing in the entry says that loquat is in the rose family's allergy group. Its allergy proteins are close kin to those in peach and apple (the lipid transfer protein and birch-pollen types), and reactions to loquat, including anaphylaxis, have been reported in people allergic to peach. Someone serving a guest with a peach or apple allergy needs to know that loquat is not a safe substitute. This should be stated as a fact about the fruit, not as a verdict on any dish. The definition has room: it is 869 characters, and adding this sentence keeps it under 1000.
findings.fix: Insert before the closing sentence: "Its allergy proteins are close kin to those in peach and apple, and people allergic to those fruits have reacted to loquat."

findings.claim: Small freckles on the skin are harmless.
findings.because: 'Harmless' reads as a safety verdict, and the house rule states facts rather than giving verdicts. The freckles are a cosmetic surface mark and do not affect eating quality, so a quality word says it accurately.
findings.fix: Small freckles on the skin are cosmetic.

findings.claim: so never pile them or wash them until you use them
findings.because: The "never ... until" construction reads as "do not pile them until you use them", as if piling becomes fine at the point of use. The two instructions need separate verbs: piling is never allowed, and washing waits until you use them.
findings.fix: so never pile them, and wash them only as you use them

findings.claim: at about 4 C (40 F)
findings.because: 4 C converts to 39.2 F, and the corpus pairs 4 C with 39 F (Blood Orange store: 4C (39F); Apricot: 2 to 4C (36 to 39F)). A house bracket should be the true conversion, not a rounder number.
findings.fix: at about 4 C (39 F)

findings.claim: no green at the stem end, ... a green one will never sweeten
findings.because: The same fact appears twice in one field of 239 characters, and the definition already says a green-shouldered loquat stays sour. The repeat uses space that could carry a buying fact the cook doesn't have yet: loquats clipped with a bit of stem attached have no open wound at the top and keep longer than bare fruit.
findings.fix: Reject sunken brown patches, split skin, or a boozy smell; fruit sold with a bit of stem still on keeps better than bare fruit.

findings.claim: Pull the stem and slip the skin off from that end with your fingers
findings.because: Prep must name the part people get wrong. A loquat keeps a tuft of dried calyx at the blossom end, which is dry and gritty in the mouth and has to be cut off. The field covers the stem end and the seeds but never mentions this tuft.
findings.fix: Pull the stem, nick off the dry calyx at the blossom end, and slip the skin off from the stem end

findings.claim: Eat the soft ones raw the day you get them
findings.because: The store field gives ripe loquats three to five days refrigerated, so the closing line seems to contradict it unless "soft" means past ripe. The close should say it is about the softest fruit.
findings.fix: Eat the softest raw the day you get them

findings.claim: "chutney"
findings.because: The contract asks for lowercase verbs or short noun forms of a method. Chutney is a dish, not a method, and it is not in the corpus method vocabulary. Every other method in this entry is a gerund. What the cook does to make chutney already has corpus terms: "pickling" (45 uses) or "preserving", which this entry already lists.
findings.fix: "pickling"

findings.claim: The definition opens on botany and calendar ('an evergreen tree of the rose family that flowers in autumn and winter and ripens in spring, one of the first tree fruits of the year') instead of mechanism. The contract says mechanism first.
findings.because: The definition opens on botany and calendar ('an evergreen tree of the rose family that flowers in autumn and winter and ripens in spring, one of the first tree fruits of the year') instead of mechanism. The contract says mechanism first.
findings.fix: Open on the second sentence's fact: 'Eriobotrya japonica, a rose-family pome whose sugar is set at picking: it will not sweeten off the tree, so a green shoulder stays sour.' Move the spring-ripening note into a short clause later, or leave it to season.

findings.claim: Vigna unguiculata, the cowpea, which the South calls the field pea and sorts by its seed.
findings.because: Outside the American South, and in the pulse trade, "field pea" means Pisum sativum var. arvense: the dried green or yellow pea that is sold whole or split. Merriam-Webster defines the term this way. A cook holding a bag labelled "field peas" in Canada, the UK, Australia or a split-pea aisle has a different species that cooks differently. This entry is named for that term, so it has to say which pea it means.
findings.fix: Vigna unguiculata, the cowpea: the South's field pea, not the dried Pisum pea sold under that name elsewhere, sorted by its seed.

findings.claim: Calcium and acid both firm the pectin that glues the cells together
findings.because: The two work differently. Calcium ions cross-link pectin chains into calcium pectate, so they do firm it. Acid does not firm pectin. At the near-neutral pH of the pot, pectin breaks down by beta-elimination, and acid slows that breakdown. The contract asks for the mechanism, so it should be stated correctly.
findings.fix: Calcium cross-links the pectin that glues the cells and acid slows its breakdown

findings.claim: Dried keep a year sealed; past two they cook unevenly.
findings.because: Old dried pulses develop the hard-to-cook defect: the cotyledon lignifies and pectin binds to calcium, so some seeds never soften however long they cook. "Cook unevenly" understates this. The field also leaves out the main thing that kills dried cowpeas in storage, the cowpea weevil (Callosobruchus maculatus), whose sign is small round exit holes in the seed.
findings.fix: Dried keep a year sealed; pinholes mean weevil, and old seed may never soften.

findings.claim: Shell by pressing the seam with a thumb and running it down the pod; buy them shelled when you can. Rinse and pick out the shriveled and split. Young tender pods, the snaps, go in the pot in short lengths. Skim the gray foam in the first minutes.
findings.because: Nowhere does the entry say the peas must be cooked through, yet "marinating" is listed under methods. The standard marinated field-pea salad (the Texas-caviar style) uses peas that are fully cooked first. A cook who knows English peas and snap peas as raw salad vegetables could marinate raw shelled cowpeas instead. Raw cowpea seed, fresh or dried, carries trypsin inhibitors and lectins (hemagglutinins), and heat is what inactivates them. This agrees with the Black-eyed Pea entry: no phytohemagglutinin, and an ordinary simmer handles its milder lectins. So no hard-boil warning is needed. The only thing missing is the fact that the peas are not eaten raw. "Buy them shelled when you can" is shopping advice, not knife work, so dropping it makes room for the safety sentence inside the 280-character ceiling.
findings.fix: Shell by pressing the seam with a thumb and running it down the pod. Rinse and pick out the shriveled and split. Snaps, the young pods, go in short lengths. Skim the gray foam early. Raw peas carry lectins and trypsin inhibitors: cook them through before dressing a salad. (272 characters; "marinating" can then stay in methods.)

findings.claim: "Vigna unguiculata, the cowpea, which the South calls the field pea and sorts by its seed. CROWDERS pack their pods ... the Black-eyed Pea is one group among many. The difference in the pot is the seed coat: a pigmented coat leaches phenolics that darken and flavor the liquor, a pale one leaches almost none."
findings.because: The contract says MECHANISM FIRST. The definition opens with about 420 characters of cultivar catalog, and the mechanism, the seed coat, only arrives in the third sentence. At 965 characters it also runs past the 650 to 950 aim. Leading with the seed coat fixes the order and trims the bridging clause.
findings.fix: "The seed coat decides the pot: a pigmented one leaches phenolics that darken and flavor the liquor, a pale one almost none. Vigna unguiculata, the cowpea, which the South calls the field pea, is sorted by it. CROWDERS pack their pods ... the Black-eyed Pea is one group among many." (Keep the crowder, cream and purple hull clauses as they are, and delete the separate "The difference in the pot is the seed coat" sentence.)

findings.claim: "which the South calls the field pea"
findings.because: Outside the American South, and in the pulse trade, "field pea" means Pisum sativum grown for dry seed: the green and yellow split pea. A cook who looks this up holding a bag of split peas lands on the wrong plant, and nothing in the entry tells them.
findings.fix: "which the South calls the field pea (elsewhere the name means the dried Pisum split pea)"

findings.claim: "Calcium and acid both firm the pectin that glues the cells together"
findings.because: Calcium does firm pectin, by cross-linking it. Acid does something different: it slows the breakdown and dissolving of pectin and hemicellulose. "Both firm" treats the two as one mechanism, and the conclusion (hard water or an early tomato stalls the peas) is still right.
findings.fix: "Calcium and acid both keep the pectin that glues the cells from dissolving"

findings.claim: "Dried keep a year sealed; past two they cook unevenly."
findings.because: It leaves the second year unaccounted for, so a cook with 18-month-old peas can't tell which rule applies. The real fact is that old dried seed hardens and cooks unevenly the longer it sits.
findings.fix: "Dried keep a year sealed; older seed hardens and cooks unevenly."

findings.claim: "buy them shelled when you can"
findings.because: This is buying advice, which belongs in choose. The contract gives prep to the knife reality and the part people get wrong, and the words are spent on neither.
findings.fix: "drop any with weevil holes"

findings.claim: "braising"
findings.because: Field peas are simmered or stewed in pot liquor. Nobody braises them: there is no sear and no part-submerged cook. Listing it next to simmering and stewing adds a method no cook would use for this ingredient.
findings.fix: Remove "braising" and keep: simmering, stewing, blanching, marinating, frying.

findings.claim: store says fresh shelled peas should be cooked 'within 3 days'. The existing Black-eyed Pea entry, which covers the same fresh shelled field peas, says 'refrigerate and cook within 2 days'. The definition also adds 'elsewhere the name means the dried Pisum pea, whole or split', but every structured field and the season describe only the Southern cowpea, so a reader looking up the Pisum split pea gets cowpea handling.
findings.because: store says fresh shelled peas should be cooked 'within 3 days'. The existing Black-eyed Pea entry, which covers the same fresh shelled field peas, says 'refrigerate and cook within 2 days'. The definition also adds 'elsewhere the name means the dried Pisum pea, whole or split', but every structured field and the season describe only the Southern cowpea, so a reader looking up the Pisum split pea gets cowpea handling.
findings.fix: Change store to 'cook within 2 days', matching Black-eyed Pea. Cut the Pisum clause, or reduce it to 'not the dried Pisum field pea of split-pea soup', so the entry clearly covers the cowpea only.

findings.claim: Boil uncovered in plenty of fresh water for 15 minutes and drain again, then finish them in the pot where the ham hock has been simmering.
findings.because: The published figures do not support 15 minutes. An open boil in a large excess of water takes out about 80 percent of the cyanide only after more than 30 minutes, and a 30 minute boil removes 97 to 99.8 percent. The one short-boil method on record needs a 24 to 48 hour soak first, not 8 to 12 hours. The line also contradicts the definition, which calls for a cook in plenty of fresh water 'that is drained off too'. Moving the beans into the hock liquor after 15 minutes means the liquid people eat is not the leaching water. Fresh shelled limas also hold linamarin, and the prep never says to cook and drain them.
findings.fix: Soak dried ones 8 to 12 hours and pour the water away. Boil them uncovered in plenty of fresh water for at least 30 minutes, drain, then finish in the hock pot. Boil fresh ones uncovered and drain too.

findings.claim: Dried: a plump half-moon with a white eye and fine ridges fanning from it. A flatter, thick skinned bean with a dark scar is a dried FAVA BEAN
findings.because: The shape tell is backwards. A dried lima, and the large butter bean most of all, is described as flat. The dried fava is the thicker, chunkier seed, usually tan to brown, and its hilum is a long black scar at one end. The lima's eye sits midway along the inner curve. So the reliable tells are where the eye sits and what color it is, not flat against plump. A cook told to look for 'the flatter one' would pick the lima as the fava.
findings.fix: Dried: a flat, smooth, cream half-moon, its white eye midway along the inner curve with fine ridges fanning from it. A thicker tan bean with a long black scar at one end is a dried FAVA BEAN

findings.claim: one species under two names: the small green baby lima and the large cream butter bean.
findings.because: How the names split between small and large beans depends on region, not botany. In the US South, including the Georgia, Alabama and Mississippi of the brief's own plate, 'butter bean' usually means the small or speckled limas. Only in Britain is the butter bean the large dried cream bean. The small beans are the sieva type and the large ones the Fordhook or big-seeded type, all Phaseolus lunatus. As written, the entry contradicts the plate it sits beside.
findings.fix: one species under many names: baby lima, Fordhook, and butter bean, which in the South means the small ones and in Britain the large dried cream ones.

findings.claim: its own enzyme, linamarase, splits it to hydrogen cyanide
findings.because: Linamarase does not release HCN directly. It hydrolyzes linamarin to glucose and acetone cyanohydrin, which then breaks down to HCN and acetone, quickly above about pH 5 or with hydroxynitrile lyase. That second step is why cyanide can still form after the enzyme is gone. The definition's next point, that heat kills the enzyme but leaves linamarin, only makes full sense with it.
findings.fix: its own enzyme, linamarase, starts it breaking down to hydrogen cyanide

findings.claim: a ten minute hard boil settles the lectin, but heat kills the enzyme and leaves the linamarin in the bean.
findings.because: This is true, but a cook is left not knowing why leftover linamarin matters once the bean's own enzyme is dead. Gut bacteria carry beta-glucosidases that can still release cyanide from linamarin eaten in the bean. That is the fact that makes the water step necessary rather than optional.
findings.fix: a ten minute hard boil settles the lectin, but heat kills the enzyme and leaves linamarin that gut bacteria can still split.

findings.claim: warmth and damp, not the calendar, cause the hard-to-cook defect
findings.because: The hard-to-cook defect builds up over storage time. High temperature and humidity speed it up sharply, but age alone still contributes, and old beans kept cool and dry still cook more slowly. 'Not the calendar' overstates the case.
findings.fix: warmth and damp, far more than age, cause the hard-to-cook defect

findings.claim: Shell fresh ones by splitting the pod seam with a thumb.
findings.because: Fresh green limas (and frozen baby limas, which are only blanched) hold linamarin too, and unlike fresh peas or small favas they must never go raw into a salad or crudite. The hint says raw beans are always cooked, but the entry only gives a cooking step for dried beans.
findings.fix: Shell fresh ones by splitting the pod seam with a thumb, and boil them, never raw.

findings.claim: Boil uncovered in plenty of fresh water for 15 minutes and drain again, then finish them in the pot where the ham hock has been simmering.
findings.because: Once the boil kills linamarase, the linamarin left in the seed comes out only slowly, by leaching as the bean softens. Fifteen minutes removes part of it, and the rest then goes into the ham hock pot liquor, which is served. The hint calls for a long uncovered cook in fresh water that is poured away. The definition says 'cook ... in plenty of fresh water that is drained off', so the prep's 15-minute boil undercuts it.
findings.fix: Boil uncovered in plenty of fresh water until nearly tender and drain again, then finish them in the pot where the ham hock has been simmering.

findings.claim: heat kills the enzyme and leaves the linamarin in the bean
findings.because: The entry never says why leftover linamarin matters, so a cook can read 'enzyme dead' as 'no cyanide'. Gut bacteria carry beta-glucosidases that still split linamarin and release cyanide after the bean is eaten. That is why the water steps are needed at all.
findings.fix: heat kills the enzyme and leaves the linamarin, which gut bacteria can still split, in the bean

findings.claim: Commercial pale varieties are low in it; dark seeded types run far higher.
findings.because: This states the hazard but gives the cook nothing to do, and 'pale varieties are low' can be read as permission to skip the water steps. Black and deep-purple seeded limas (the wild and tropical types sold as Java, Burma or Rangoon beans) can hold many times the cyanogen of the bred white and green types, and the ordinary soak and boil is not reliably enough for them. The tell belongs where the bean is in the cook's hand.
findings.fix: Bred cream and green types are low in it; black or purple seeded ones run many times higher, so pass them by. Keep the soak and boil either way.

findings.claim: whose vicine brings on favism in G6PD deficiency: check loose bins
findings.because: Vicine and convicine are both implicated, and the existing Fava Bean entry names both. Both are heat stable: the Fava Bean entry says 'cooking does not destroy them'. Next to a definition that says the soak and boil takes lima toxins out, a cook could assume the same water treatment makes a mistaken fava harmless. It does not.
findings.fix: whose vicine and convicine bring on favism in G6PD deficiency, cooked or not: check loose bins

findings.claim: "Boil uncovered in plenty of fresh water for 15 minutes and drain again, then finish them in the pot where the ham hock has been simmering."
findings.because: This contradicts the definition, which says the beans cook in plenty of fresh water "that is drained off too", and the hint, which asks for a long uncovered cook whose water is also poured away. A 15 minute parboil followed by a finish in hock liquor that gets served is not that. "Drain again" also points only at the dried beans, so fresh shelled limas, which hold linamarin too, get no cooking step at all.
findings.fix: "Cook fresh or dried uncovered in plenty of fresh water until tender and drain, then finish them with the simmered ham hock."

findings.claim: "For succotash, the ham hock simmers from the start and the corn goes in only for the last five minutes."
findings.because: Two sentences earlier the entry says the cooking water is drained off. "From the start" does not say which pot the hock is in, so a cook can read it as simmering the hock in the bean water, which is exactly the water the entry says to pour away.
findings.fix: "For succotash, simmer the ham hock from the start in its own pot, add the drained beans, and the corn only for the last five minutes."

findings.claim: "What takes both out is water. Linamarin and cyanide dissolve, so"
findings.because: The sentence just before names the lectin and the linamarin, so "both" reads as those two. Water does not remove the lectin; heat does. The pair meant here is linamarin and cyanide, and the reader only learns that one sentence later.
findings.fix: "Water is the fix: linamarin and cyanide both dissolve, so"

findings.claim: "one species under two names: the small green baby lima and the large cream butter bean"
findings.because: The plate this entry sits on, Southeastern Vegetables, uses "Butter Beans" for the fresh summer bean of Georgia, Alabama and Mississippi. In the American South, "butter bean" is the regional name for fresh limas of any size, not only the large cream dried type (that narrower meaning is the British one). As written, the entry contradicts the plate a cook will read it against.
findings.fix: "one species under two names, lima and, in the South and Britain, butter bean: small green baby limas and large types that dry to cream"

findings.claim: "Dried: a plump half-moon with a white eye and fine ridges fanning from it."
findings.because: The contract asks choose to name the specific defect to reject. The fresh half of the field does that; the dried half only describes a good bean. The compound adjective should also be hyphenated, as the corpus does with "thin-skinned".
findings.fix: "Fresh pods plump, green and firm; reject yellowed or limp ones. Dried: plump half-moons, a white eye, fine ridges fanning from it; reject cracked or wrinkled. A flatter, thick-skinned bean with a dark scar is a dried FAVA BEAN, whose vicine brings on favism in G6PD deficiency." (277 characters)

findings.claim: "Shell fresh ones by splitting the pod seam with a thumb."
findings.because: Lima pods are flat, leathery and tough, not like pea pods. A thumb often will not open the seam, and this is the knife reality that the contract says prep must get right.
findings.fix: "Shell fresh ones by tearing the tough seam open or snipping the curved edge."

findings.claim: "dark seeded types run far higher"
findings.because: A compound adjective before a noun takes a hyphen; the corpus writes "thin-skinned" (Cannellini Bean). A hyphen is not a dash, so the house rule allows it.
findings.fix: "dark-seeded types run far higher"

findings.claim: Roasted, spread to cool and freeze the same day with the skins on, as the Hatch Chile entry sets out
findings.because: The Hatch Chile entry does not say 'the same day'. It says the pods must be cold within 2 hours of the roaster and in the freezer within two hours, because roasted chile is low acid and a sealed warm bag is airless. 'The same day' lets a warm bag sit for hours, and the entry claims agreement with a rule it actually loosens.
findings.fix: Roasted, spread to cool and freeze within 2 hours with the skins on, as the Hatch Chile entry sets out

findings.claim: the honest answer is meat and heat against sweetness and earth
findings.because: The plate's correction reads Pueblo as 'medium hot, earthy, meaty'. Giving 'earth' to Hatch as the contrast contradicts that correction. Seed sellers also describe Mosco's flavor as sweet, so sweetness does not separate the two chiles either. The real difference is the wall and the heat.
findings.fix: the honest answer: more wall and more heat, the same roasted earth

findings.claim: the pods grow pointing up off the plant instead of hanging
findings.because: Colorado State and seed-house descriptions of Mosco say the fruit grows upright but may bend downward as pods reach full size and weight. Mature and red pods often hang, so a cook or buyer cannot use orientation as a firm field mark.
findings.fix: the pods set pointing up off the plant, drooping only when full and heavy

findings.claim: MOSCO is the named cultivar, a family seed line kept for generations in the Arkansas Valley around Pueblo, Colorado.
findings.because: Mosco is not simply a family line. Dr. Michael Bartolo of Colorado State University's Arkansas Valley Research Center selected and improved it in the 1990s from a strain his uncle Harry Mosco grew on the St. Charles Mesa, then named it and released it to growers. It is also not the only Pueblo chile grown: other family strains are sold as Pueblo chile too.
findings.fix: MOSCO is the best-known cultivar, a Colorado State selection from one family's Arkansas Valley seed line.

findings.claim: Fresh, a week in the crisper, dry and unbagged.
