findings.because: Fresh chiles keep best at high humidity (UC Davis postharvest: about 7.5 C (45 F), 90 to 95 percent relative humidity). Loose in a fridge they lose water and wrinkle within the week, which is the very defect the choose field tells the cook to reject. The right advice is dry, in a paper or perforated bag, which lets out condensation without drying the pod.
findings.fix: Fresh, a week in the crisper, dry, in a paper or perforated bag.

findings.claim: Peel after roasting: sweat the pods in a covered bowl 10 minutes and the skin slides off.
findings.because: The store field and the Hatch Chile entry both say to freeze the pods skins on and peel only what you are about to cook. A cook who follows prep literally peels the whole batch after roasting and freezes bare pods, which undoes the storage advice.
findings.fix: Peel only what you will cook: fresh-roasted after 10 minutes sweating in a covered bowl, frozen as the pod softens.

findings.claim: the pod takes a hard char in the September drum roasters
findings.because: The entry's own season is August to October, and so is the plate's. Pueblo roasting begins in August with the harvest and runs to the first frost. September is the festival month, not the whole roasting season, so the sentence reads as if roasters run only in September.
findings.fix: the pod takes a hard char in the late-summer drum roasters

findings.claim: Roasted, spread to cool and freeze the same day with the skins on, as the Hatch Chile entry sets out
findings.because: The Hatch Chile entry doesn't say "the same day". It says the chile must be cold within 2 hours of the roaster (store) and in the freezer within two hours (definition). Its reason is that roasted chile is low acid and a sealed warm bag has no air. "The same day" lets a warm 10 to 20 kg sack of roasted chile, bought hot at the September drum roasters, sit in a car or on a counter for hours in the 5 to 57 C (41 to 135 F) range. That is the hazard the Hatch entry was written to close. This field also cites Hatch while contradicting it, and it drops Hatch's safe refrigerated option (3 days).
findings.fix: Roasted, spread in one layer and cold within 2 hours of the roaster, then 3 days refrigerated or a year frozen with the skins on, as the Hatch Chile entry sets out.

findings.claim: Never keep roasted chile under oil at room temperature: low acid and airless is where botulism grows.
findings.because: Saying "at room temperature" suggests that chile under oil is safe in the fridge for as long as you like. It isn't. Non-proteolytic Clostridium botulinum grows slowly from about 3 C (38 F), and a line fridge opened all service often runs warmer. The standard guidance for low-acid vegetables in oil is to refrigerate and use within about 4 days, or freeze. Cooks keep a quart of roasted chile in oil in the walk-in for weeks, and this sentence doesn't stop them.
findings.fix: Roasted chile under oil lives in the fridge and is used within 4 days, or frozen: low acid and airless is where botulism grows.

findings.claim: Wear gloves, since this one is hotter than it looks, and taste a strip first.
findings.because: The entry has the cook give a medium-hot pod a hard char (the methods list charring and roasting). Blistering hot chile over an open flame or under a broiler puts capsaicin into the smoke and steam, and in a closed kitchen that makes people cough and burns their eyes. The gloves note covers the hands but not the air, and it doesn't say what happens after the gloves come off: eyes and contact lenses.
findings.fix: Char under a running hood; the smoke carries capsaicin. Wear gloves, since this one is hotter than it looks, and keep hands off eyes until washed. Taste a strip first.

findings.claim: Roasted, spread to cool and freeze the same day with the skins on, as the Hatch Chile entry sets out
findings.because: The Hatch Chile entry does not say 'the same day'. It says cold within 2 hours of the roaster, because roasted chile is low acid and a sealed warm bag is airless. 'The same day' allows hours in the danger zone, and then credits that looser rule to an entry that says something stricter. So the entry misquotes its own cross-reference on the safety point.
findings.fix: Roasted, spread in one layer, cold within 2 hours and frozen with the skins on, as the Hatch Chile entry sets out; a year frozen.

findings.claim: The working difference from a Hatch is the wall: thick and meaty
findings.because: The related Hatch Chile entry tells the cook to choose 'thick-walled pods'. Calling the wall the working difference, with Pueblo as the thick one, suggests Hatch is thin-walled and contradicts that entry. What growers claim for Pueblo is a thicker, meatier wall, which is a matter of degree.
findings.fix: The working difference from a Hatch is the wall: thicker and meatier

findings.claim: the honest answer is meat and heat against sweetness and earth
findings.because: This gives 'earth' to New Mexico and none to Pueblo. The plate correction the entry must not contradict says to read Pueblo as 'medium hot, earthy, meaty'. The contrast the facts support is Pueblo's wall and heat against Hatch's sweetness, and both chiles are earthy.
findings.fix: the honest answer is more wall and more heat against a sweeter pod

findings.claim: Heat runs medium hot, well above mild Hatch cultivars such as Big Jim
findings.because: All three exemplars and the related chile entries give heat as a Scoville range; Hatch Chile puts Big Jim at 500 to 2,500. Without a number, 'medium hot' and 'well above' cannot be checked against the Hatch entry. The plate correction's source gives Mosco roughly 5,000 to 20,000 Scoville.
findings.fix: Heat runs about 5,000 to 20,000 Scoville, well above a Big Jim Hatch

findings.claim: A Mirasol-type chile, the name meaning it looks at the sun: the pods grow pointing up off the plant instead of hanging. MOSCO is the named cultivar, a family seed line kept for generations in the Arkansas Valley around Pueblo, Colorado.
findings.because: The contract says MECHANISM FIRST and no history for its own sake. The opening two sentences are etymology and provenance, 244 characters, and the mechanism the cook uses (the thick wall that lets steam lift the skin and keeps the pod whole in a stew) does not arrive until the third sentence.
findings.fix: A thick-walled Mirasol-type chile from around Pueblo, Colorado, pods pointing up at the sun, which is what mirasol means; MOSCO is the named cultivar.

findings.claim: and taste a strip first
findings.because: The definition already closes on 'Taste one strip from every bag before you season the pot'. The prep repeats it and spends characters the knife reality needs, such as keeping the juice that pools under the peeled pods, which the Hatch entry calls the sauce.
findings.fix: and keep the juice that pools under the pods

findings.claim: "peeling"
findings.because: Methods lists the ways a cook cooks the item (the exemplars and Hatch Chile list roasting, charring, stuffing, stewing and grilling). Peeling is a prep step, and the prep field already covers it.
findings.fix: Remove "peeling" from methods.

findings.claim: a dense mesh of hyphae that will become spores
findings.because: The hyphae do not turn into spores. In puffballs the gleba's hyphae carry basidia, and the basidia produce the spores. The hyphae stay behind as capillitium threads in the ripe powder.
findings.fix: a dense mesh of hyphae whose basidia will bear spores

findings.claim: in most species a sterile, chambered subgleba sits at the base. Calvatia gigantea, the giant, can pass the size of a football
findings.because: MushroomExpert describes Calvatia gigantea as "without a sterile basal area". The entry's headline species therefore lacks the subgleba that the sentence just before it leads the cook to look for at the base.
findings.fix: in most small species a sterile, chambered subgleba sits at the base, though the giant has none. Calvatia gigantea can pass the size of a football

findings.claim: Lycoperdon and the smaller Calvatia run golf ball to fist
findings.because: Lycoperdon perlatum and its kin run about 2 to 6 cm, which fits. The other common Calvatia, C. cyathiformis and C. craniiformis, usually run 7 to 20 cm, the size of a grapefruit or a small melon, which is well past a fist.
findings.fix: Lycoperdon runs golf ball to egg, the other Calvatia fist to melon

findings.claim: Any yellow means past.
findings.because: Yellow then olive is how C. gigantea and Lycoperdon ripen. The purple-spored puffball Calvatia cyathiformis ripens through lilac to purple-brown and never turns yellow. A cook who is watching only for yellow can pass a tinted face.
findings.fix: Any tint at all, yellow, olive or purple, means past.

findings.claim: Any outline of a cap, gills or stem means a young Amanita button, whose amatoxins survive cooking.
findings.because: A button with a cap-and-gill outline can belong to any gilled mushroom, for example Agaricus, Chlorophyllum or Amanita muscaria. Amatoxins are carried only by the death cap and destroying-angel group, not by every Amanita. The rule to discard is right, but the stated identification overclaims. Safety facts should be stated about the fungus accurately.
findings.fix: Any outline of a cap, gills or stem means a gilled mushroom's button, possibly a death cap or destroying angel, whose amatoxins survive cooking.

findings.claim: The earthball, Scleroderma, is white inside when very young too; know it by its thick, hard, ochre-yellow, scaly rind.
findings.because: The sentence tells the cook how to recognize an earthball but never says why that matters. Scleroderma citrinum is poisonous and causes severe gastrointestinal illness. It also turns purple-black inside very quickly, so any dark marbling is a second sign.
findings.fix: The poisonous earthball, Scleroderma, is white inside when very young too; know it by its thick, hard, ochre-yellow, scaly rind and any purple-black marbling.

findings.claim: then liver failure follows on days two to four
findings.because: Clinical sources place the start of the hepatic phase at 36 to 48 hours, with jaundice on day 3 or 4. Frank liver failure and death usually come later, around days 4 to 9. The current wording suggests the danger has passed after day four.
findings.fix: then liver damage shows from day two to four and can end in liver failure within the week

findings.claim: The test is the cut. Halve every specimen top to bottom and read the face: it must be pure white and uniform, like fresh bread or marshmallow, edge to edge. Any yellow means past. Any outline of a cap, gills or stem means a young Amanita button, whose amatoxins survive cooking.
findings.because: The definition presents the white cut face as the whole test, but a very young earthball (Scleroderma) also cuts white and shows no cap, gill or stem outline, so it passes every check the definition gives. The rind check that catches it appears only in choose, and a cook who reads only the definition misses it. On the cut face a puffball shows a skin as thin as paper. An earthball shows a hard rind millimeters thick as a separate band, and its firm interior soon marbles purple-black.
findings.fix: Add one sentence after the Amanita sentence: "A hard rind millimeters thick on the cut face, around a firm interior, means an earthball."

findings.claim: Heavy, firm, springy
findings.because: Heavy and firm are exactly how an earthball feels: a dense, hard, rigid ball like a small potato. A good puffball feels firm but gives and springs back like marshmallow. Leading with "heavy, firm" steers the cook toward the look-alike.
findings.fix: Firm but springy like marshmallow, never hard or rigid

findings.claim: know it by its thick, hard, ochre-yellow, scaly rind
findings.because: Ochre-yellow and scaly describes only Scleroderma citrinum. S. areolatum, S. verrucosum and S. cepa are brown and smoother or only finely cracked, so a cook who looks for yellow scales will pass a brown earthball. The check that holds for the whole genus is a thick, hard rind that shows as a distinct layer on the cut face, plus an interior that soon turns purple-gray to black.
findings.fix: know it by its thick, hard rind, a distinct band on the cut face, yellowish to brown and scaly or cracked, around a firm interior that soon marbles purple-black

findings.claim: Amatoxin symptoms start 6 to 24 hours after the meal, ease falsely, then liver failure follows on days two to four.
findings.because: The timeline is correct, but it leaves out what the cook has to do with it. The dangerous part is that the easing looks like recovery, and the late onset means nobody links the illness to the meal. Keeping one uncooked specimen from each batch is the standard forager's practice, because it lets a poison center identify the mushroom. The field has room: it is at 473 of 700 characters.
findings.fix: Amatoxin symptoms start 6 to 24 hours after the meal and ease falsely; the easing is not recovery, and liver failure follows on days two to four. Keep one raw specimen back from every batch.

findings.claim: so cut it again before cooking and discard any yellowed part
findings.because: This contradicts the definition, which says "Any yellow means past" and treats yellow as a verdict on the whole specimen. Here the cook is told to trim the yellow and cook the rest. The tissue next to a yellowed patch is further into ripening than it looks, and ripening gleba is what upsets the gut.
findings.fix: so cut it again before cooking and discard it if any face has yellowed

findings.claim: "Whole and uncut in a paper bag at 2 to 4 C (36 to 39 F), one to two days: ... so cut it again before cooking"
findings.because: Choose and d both tell the cook to halve every specimen top to bottom before accepting it, so no checked puffball is still whole and uncut when it reaches storage. The field contradicts the test the entry depends on, and "cut it again" assumes a cut that "uncut" rules out.
findings.fix: "Halved for the check, in a paper bag at 2 to 4 C (36 to 39 F), one to two days: the spores keep ripening after picking, so cut a fresh face before cooking"

findings.claim: "Any outline of a cap, gills or stem means a young Amanita button, whose amatoxins survive cooking."
findings.because: A cap, gill or stem outline shows that the cook is holding the egg-stage button of a gilled mushroom. That button may be an Amanita, but it can also be an Agaricus or another genus. The action is the same either way (throw it out), but the categorical "means" states something that isn't true. The rule is to be right, and the safety fact has to be stated as a fact about the fungus.
findings.fix: "Any outline of a cap, gills or stem means a gilled button, possibly an Amanita, whose amatoxins survive cooking."

findings.claim: The whole field, 473 characters, including "each face pure white and uniform, no cap, gill or stem outline" and "smelling clean and mushroomy"
findings.because: The contract sets 140 to 280 characters. Going past that up to 700 is allowed, but only for the look-alike material, as with matsutake. The earthball and amatoxin sentences earn the overage. The white-face and outline test is repeated almost word for word from d ("pure white and uniform", "outline of a cap, gills or stem"), so part of the length is repetition, not safety.
findings.fix: "Heavy, firm, springy, skin intact, smelling clean. Halve every one top to bottom, small Lycoperdon above all, where an Amanita egg hides. The earthball, Scleroderma, is white inside when very young; know it by its thick, hard, ochre-yellow, scaly rind. Amatoxin symptoms start 6 to 24 hours after the meal, ease falsely, then liver failure follows on days two to four."

findings.claim: "can pass the size of a football"
findings.because: The corpus is written in American English, and to an American reader "football" means an American football, not the round soccer ball the comparison intends. A giant puffball is a rough sphere, and large ones reach well past soccer-ball size.
findings.fix: "can pass the size of a basketball"

findings.claim: is dominated by eugenol, the same phenol that drives clove, which is why jerk reads as clove, cinnamon and nutmeg at once
findings.because: Eugenol (about 65 to 85 percent of allspice berry oil) explains the clove note only. The pepper and nutmeg edges come from minor compounds: beta-caryophyllene gives the pepper and 1,8-cineole the camphor-nutmeg note, with methyl eugenol alongside. In jerk, the cinnamon and nutmeg are also simply added, as the next sentence of the entry says. As written, one phenol is credited with three spices, which is a mechanism error.
findings.fix: is dominated by eugenol, the same phenol that drives clove, so it reads as clove; caryophyllene and cineole add pepper

findings.claim: Wear gloves for the Scotch bonnets:
findings.because: Capsaicin passes through latex, and the related Habanero entry already says nitrile, not latex. A wet paste is made by blending the bonnets, and blending throws capsaicin into the air. The Scotch Bonnet and Habanero entries both warn about this: lift the blender lid away from your face. The entry for the paste, the one place a cook actually blends bonnets, leaves both points out.
findings.fix: Wear nitrile gloves for the Scotch bonnets and open the blender away from your face:

findings.claim: Salt or sugar listed first on the label means filler.
findings.because: This works for a wet paste: good jarred pastes list scallion or hot pepper first. On a dry rub, salt is normally the largest ingredient by weight, even in a good blend. Most commercial dry jerk rubs read 'salt, sugar, spices', so the rule would have a cook reject almost every dry rub. It also overlaps with the next sentence, which already covers a dry rub that smells mostly of salt.
findings.fix: A paste label should lead with scallion or pepper; salt or sugar first means filler.

findings.claim: fresh garlic under oil never sits out
findings.because: Fresh scallion and ginger are low-acid aromatics in the same blend, so they carry the same botulism concern under an oily paste. The related Scallion entry names scallion in oil as 'the botulism setup'. Singling out garlic suggests the rest of the paste is safe at room temperature.
findings.fix: fresh garlic and scallion under oil never sit out

findings.claim: Slash chicken to the bone, work the paste in, and marinate 12 to 24 hours. Wipe off the excess before the grill or it burns.
findings.because: A 12 to 24 hour marinade on raw chicken belongs in the refrigerator, and the entry never says so. The paste wiped off has been in contact with raw poultry. A cook who keeps it back to baste or serve alongside carries raw-chicken bacteria onto cooked meat. As written, the only reason given for wiping it off is burning.
findings.fix: Gloves for the Scotch bonnets: capsaicin sits in the pale ribs and water will not lift it from skin; wash with soap. Slash chicken to the bone, work the paste in, refrigerate 12 to 24 hours. Wipe off and discard the excess: it has touched raw chicken, and on the grill it burns.

findings.claim: Brown sugar scorches over open flame, so cook over indirect heat and finish over the coals.
findings.because: The typical jerk failure is a blackened sugar-and-spice crust over chicken that is still raw at the bone. Slashing to the bone helps but does not solve it. The dark crust looks done well before the thickest thigh meat is. The sentence gives the heat method but no doneness point, so a cook can take the color as the signal.
findings.fix: Brown sugar blackens long before the meat at the bone is done, so cook over indirect heat to 74 C (165 F) at the bone, then finish over the coals.

findings.claim: Homemade paste keeps about a week in the refrigerator or three months frozen; fresh garlic under oil never sits out.
findings.because: The hazard is Clostridium botulinum spores on fresh low-acid aromatics (scallion and ginger as well as garlic) sealed from air by oil. The lime or vinegar in the paste is what inhibits them. A week is reasonable only for the acidified paste the definition describes. An oil-only paste without the acid should follow the usual garlic-in-oil limit of about four days refrigerated. Naming only garlic also understates what the risk covers.
findings.fix: Unopened jarred paste keeps a year in the cupboard; refrigerate once opened and use within a few months. Homemade paste keeps a week refrigerated with its lime or vinegar, four days without, or three months frozen; never leave it out. Dry rub keeps six months airtight and dark.

findings.claim: Salt or sugar listed first on the label means filler. Reject a dry rub that smells of little but salt, and any jar with a bulging lid.
findings.because: Many jarred jerk pastes and marinades, and many restaurant and home recipes, add soy sauce, which brings soy and usually wheat. The definition's list (allspice, Scotch bonnet, thyme, scallion, garlic, ginger, sugar, nutmeg, cinnamon) and its line that the rest is negotiable let a cook assume the paste has neither. The label is the one place to catch this, and this field already sends the cook to the label. The fact should be stated plainly, not as a verdict that any paste is free of anything.
findings.fix: Green-brown, smelling first of scallion, thyme and clove-sweet allspice, Scotch bonnet close behind. Salt or sugar first on the label means filler. Many pastes add soy sauce, so soy and often wheat: read the label. Reject any jar with a bulging lid.

findings.claim: "is dominated by eugenol, the same phenol that drives clove, which is why jerk reads as clove, cinnamon and nutmeg at once"
findings.because: Eugenol explains the clove note and nothing more. Cinnamon's signature is cinnamaldehyde. Allspice's "cabinet" impression comes from eugenol together with methyleugenol, caryophyllene and other terpenes. The same entry also lists real cinnamon and nutmeg among the fillers, so crediting one phenol for those notes contradicts the next sentence.
findings.fix: "is dominated by eugenol, the same phenol that drives clove, which is why jerk reads first of clove"

findings.claim: "fresh garlic under oil never sits out"
findings.because: Nothing in the entry describes the paste as oil-based. The definition blends it with scallion and lime or vinegar, so a cook making an oil-free paste will think the warning does not apply. The real hazard is any low-acid paste of raw garlic, scallion and ginger kept sealed from air, oil or not.
findings.fix: "raw garlic and scallion paste never sits out"

findings.claim: "Wear gloves for the Scotch bonnets: the capsaicin sits in the pale ribs, and water alone will not lift it from skin, so wash with soap after."
findings.because: This repeats what the existing Scotch Bonnet entry already says in its definition and prep: gloves, the burn in the placenta, capsaicin does not rinse off, use soap. The rule is to cross-reference an existing entry by name and not repeat it, and prep space should go to what is particular to the paste.
findings.fix: "Handle the Scotch bonnets as that entry says; scraping or keeping the pith sets the heat."

findings.claim: "Capsaicin dissolves in fat and alcohol rather than water and survives cooking, so the heat that goes on the meat stays on it."
findings.because: The fat-solubility half repeats The Three Heats entry. The part that is new here is that capsaicin survives the fire. Cutting the repeat also brings the definition from 955 characters back inside the 650 to 950 aim.
findings.fix: "Capsaicin survives the fire, so the heat that goes on the meat stays on it."

findings.claim: "Its working parts are fat soluble ... That is why it is bloomed in fat before liquid goes in, and why a stale jar goes from brick red to brown and tastes of dust."
findings.because: Being fat soluble explains the bloom, but it does not explain the browning. A stale jar goes brown because the carotenoids oxidize (driven by oxygen, light, heat and moisture) and because browning compounds form as the powder warms and takes up water. As written, the sentence gives fat solubility as the cause of both.
findings.fix: Split the causes: "That is why it is bloomed in fat before liquid goes in. Air, heat and damp oxidize the carotenoids and brown the powder, so a stale jar turns from brick red to brown and tastes of dust."

findings.claim: "Light and air bleach the carotenoids first, so a clear jar on a sunny shelf goes brown fastest."
findings.because: Light and oxygen fade paprika-type powders: the color goes pale and dull. The shift toward brown comes mainly from heat and humidity, with browning compounds forming alongside the carotenoid loss. Saying the powder is bleached and then goes brown contradicts itself, and it puts the browning on the wrong cause. The stove clause earlier in the field is the one that names the browning risk correctly.
findings.fix: "Light and air fade the carotenoids and heat and damp brown them, so a clear jar on a sunny shelf by the stove spoils fastest."

findings.claim: "Brick red and loose ... Reject brown powder"
findings.because: The entry says the base is mostly ancho, and freshly ground ancho is a deep mahogany, reddish brown. Ancho-heavy blends with plenty of cumin can look reddish brown straight from a new jar. Going by hue alone, a cook would throw out a fresh jar. The reliable signs of a dead jar are a dull, faded, flat color together with a weak smell.
findings.fix: "Reject powder that looks dull or faded for its type, hard clumps, and a jar that smells only of dust."

findings.claim: "CHILE POWDER from a single pod, CAYENNE, and the lal mirch of Indian recipes carry no cumin"
findings.because: Pure chile powder is ground from one chile variety, not from "a single pod". The spelling also does not reliably tell the two products apart. Brands use chili, chile and chilli inconsistently, and the "chilli powder" sold in Indian and British shops is pure ground chile under nearly the same name. The only dependable test is the ingredient list, and a cook who trusts the spelling will make the exact swap error this entry is warning against.
findings.fix: "CHILE POWDER from one variety, CAYENNE, and the lal mirch of Indian recipes carry no cumin; the spelling on the jar is not reliable, so read the ingredients"

findings.claim: "Smoke is not built in; it comes only when chipotle or smoked paprika is in the mix."
findings.because: The plate prints "smoky", and the entry is right to correct it. But ancho, which the entry names as the base, has a faintly roasted, smoky, raisin-like note of its own even though it is never smoked. Some blends also add other smoked chiles such as morita, or smoke flavoring. Saying "only" overstates the point.
findings.fix: "Real smoke is not built in; it comes from chipotle, smoked paprika or added smoke, though ancho lends a faint roasted note."

findings.claim: Reject brown powder, hard clumps, and a jar that smells only of dust.
findings.because: The only rejection cue here is staleness, but the real hazard in ground dried chile is mold. Chiles dried or stored damp are a known source of aflatoxins (and ochratoxin A), which is why the EU sets aflatoxin limits specifically for Capsicum. These toxins survive heat, so blooming or braising does not remove them. A musty or damp smell is the cue a cook can actually check, and the entry leaves it out. Clumping from damp matters for the same reason.
findings.fix: Reject brown powder, hard clumps, and a jar that smells musty, of damp, or only of dust: molds on damp chile make aflatoxin, which cooking does not destroy.

findings.claim: Never shake it over a steaming pot: moisture wicks into the jar and cakes it.
findings.because: "dry rub" is listed under methods, but no field says how to keep the jar clean. A cook seasoning raw meat will reach back into the jar with contaminated fingers or a contaminated spoon. Salmonella survives for months in dry, low-moisture spices, and the jar is then used on food that may never reach a kill step. Salmonella outbreaks have been traced to red pepper and chili powder.
findings.fix: Never shake it over a steaming pot, and never reach in with hands that touched raw meat: moisture cakes the jar and dry powder keeps Salmonella alive for months. Portion a rub into a bowl first.

findings.claim: Read the label for salt, and salt the pot after the spice goes in.
findings.because: The entry points the cook at the label only for salt. A blend is where hidden ingredients live. A US label may declare its spices collectively as "spices", so celery or mustard (declarable allergens in the EU and UK, not major allergens in the US) can sit in the jar unnamed. Some blends also carry onion, sugar or anti-caking agents. The entry also teaches that the chile/chili spelling separates pure chile from the blend, but that spelling is unregulated, and some jars sold as "chile powder" contain cumin. So the label's ingredient list is the only record a kitchen has when a guest asks. Stay a fact about the product and do not give a verdict.
findings.fix: Read the ingredients, not the spelling, which is unregulated: "spices" on a US label can hide celery or mustard. Salt the pot after the spice goes in.

findings.claim: CHILE POWDER from a single pod, CAYENNE, and the lal mirch of Indian recipes carry no cumin
findings.because: This reads as a flat statement that anything labeled chile powder, cayenne or lal mirch has no cumin. For a guest avoiding cumin (a rare but documented spice allergy), a cook would use it as a verdict. It is true of pure single-chile products by definition, but the label word does not guarantee it (see the spelling finding above). Tie the claim to the product, not the name.
findings.fix: Pure ground chile (a single pod, CAYENNE, the lal mirch of Indian recipes) holds no cumin by definition and can be many times hotter

findings.claim: Brick red and loose, with chile named first on the label
findings.because: The cue for picking a good jar is its color, but ground chile is the classic target for color fraud. Illegal Sudan dyes (Sudan I to IV) set off EU emergency measures and mass recalls of chili powder, and lead compounds have been found in imported ground chile and other red spices. Neither can be seen by eye, and an unnaturally vivid red is the one visible hint. The protection is to buy from a traceable brand, not to judge the color.
findings.fix: Brick red, not neon, and loose, from a traceable brand (ground chile has been found dyed with Sudan red), with chile named first on the label

findings.claim: "Light and air bleach the carotenoids first, so a clear jar on a sunny shelf goes brown fastest."
findings.because: The entry contradicts itself. The definition says "the aromatic oils of cumin fade fastest once ground", so the carotenoids cannot also be the first thing to go. The volatile oils do go first: the jar goes flat and smells of dust before the color turns brown. Carotenoid bleaching is the later, visible sign.
findings.fix: "Light and air bleach the carotenoids, so a clear jar on a sunny shelf goes brown fastest."

findings.claim: The mechanism ("Its working parts are fat soluble: capsaicin carries the heat and red carotenoids carry the color, while the aromatic oils of cumin fade fastest once ground.") does not start until the fifth sentence, about 390 characters in.
findings.because: The contract says MECHANISM FIRST. The exemplars open with the mechanism (Coconut Milk: "Not a juice but an emulsion: ..."; Caper: glucocapparin meeting myrosinase in the first sentence). Here the opening is taken up by composition and the substitution warning.
findings.fix: Open with: "A blend, not a chile, whose working parts are fat soluble: capsaicin carries the heat, red carotenoids the color, and cumin's aromatic oils fade fastest once ground." Then continue with "The American jar holds ..." and cut the later sentence that starts "Its working parts are fat soluble". The total length stays about the same and stays within 325 to 1200.

findings.claim: "CHILE POWDER from a single pod"
findings.because: Pure chile powder is ground from a single chile variety (ancho, New Mexico, chipotle), not from one pod. A cook will read "a single pod" literally.
findings.fix: "CHILE POWDER of one variety"

findings.claim: Picking pods: dry, straw colored, snapping, sweet when chewed, taken from the tree.
findings.because: Picking pods off the tree does not by itself prevent aflatoxin. Desert Harvesters' testing found that mature pods picked after even one rain often carried high aflatoxin B1 from Aspergillus flavus, and pods picked before the summer monsoon (mid June to late July in the Sonoran Desert) tested low. They also advise never washing or wetting pods. When a pod was picked matters more than whether it came off the tree, and the entry leaves that out.
findings.fix: Picking pods: dry, straw colored, snapping, sweet when chewed, pulled from the tree before the summer rains and never washed; skip pods with dark spots or pinholes.

findings.claim: Pods left on the ground can grow Aspergillus molds that make aflatoxin, so pickers take them off the tree.
findings.because: Aflatoxin risk comes from moisture, not only from ground contact. Pods still hanging on the tree grow aflatoxin-producing Aspergillus flavus once monsoon rain wets them. As written, the sentence suggests that any pod taken from the tree is fine.
findings.fix: Pods wetted by rain, on the tree or the ground, can grow Aspergillus flavus, which makes aflatoxin, so pickers take dry pods from the tree before the summer rains.

findings.claim: the ground seed adds protein and a galactomannan gum like guar, which is why a batter thickens as it stands
findings.because: The seed is a small share of the pod. The mesocarp flour itself is about 25 to 32 percent dietary fiber, and that fiber is the main reason a mesquite batter soaks up water and stiffens. The seed galactomannan is real but adds only a little. It also differs from guar in structure: its mannose to galactose ratio is about 1.1 to 1.4, where guar's is about 2.
findings.fix: the pulp is a quarter fiber and the ground seed adds protein and a galactomannan gum, which is why a batter thickens as it stands

findings.claim: The plate files it among fruits, but nobody eats the pod fresh
findings.because: A legume pod is botanically a fruit (a dry one), so the plate is not wrong on botany; its error is suggesting the pod is eaten like fresh fruit. Also, ripe pods are chewed straight off the tree, and the entry's own choose field says 'sweet when chewed', so 'nobody eats the pod fresh' contradicts the entry. The plate correction is about how the pod is served, and this rewording keeps to it.
findings.fix: The pod is a dry fruit, not one to serve fresh; a kitchen buys the flour

findings.claim: Whole pods are too hard for a home blender
findings.because: Home cooks do grind dry pods in high-speed blenders and food processors. The pulp breaks down into a coarse meal, and the stone-hard seeds stay mostly whole, so the meal has to be sifted. A cook should hear that the job is possible but slow, with the seeds as the obstacle.
findings.fix: A home blender turns dry pod pulp into coarse meal but leaves the stone-hard seeds whole; sift them out

findings.claim: pantry moths and seed beetles finish it
findings.because: Seed beetles (bruchids) attack whole pods and seeds; their larvae develop inside intact seeds and cannot breed in milled flour. The pests of stored flour are pantry moths such as the Indian meal moth and flour beetles such as Tribolium. The next sentence about freezing pods is the right place for bruchids.
findings.fix: pantry moths and flour beetles finish it

findings.claim: Freeze picked pods for a few days before milling to kill beetle eggs in the seeds.
findings.because: Bruchid eggs are laid on the outside of the pod. The larvae bore into the seeds, and those larvae are what milling carries into the flour. Freezing kills both, so the wording should name both stages.
findings.fix: Freeze picked pods for a few days before milling to kill beetle eggs and larvae.

findings.claim: "grilling", "smoking"
findings.because: Grilling and smoking belong to the mesquite wood, not to the pod, flour or syrup, which is the ingredient this entry covers. The definition itself says 'the flour carries none of it'. Listing these verbs tells a cook that mesquite flour is grilled or smoked.
findings.fix: ["baking", "toasting", "whisking", "simmering", "reducing"]

findings.claim: Pods left on the ground can grow Aspergillus molds that make aflatoxin, so pickers take them off the tree.
findings.because: Picking from the tree lowers the risk but does not remove it. Pods still hanging when summer (monsoon) rains arrive can also mold and carry aflatoxin, which is why harvest guidance is to pick dry pods before the rains. Aflatoxin also survives heat, so baking, toasting or boiling the syrup does not destroy it. As written, a cook concludes that 'off the tree' means clean, and nothing warns that cooking will not fix a moldy batch.
findings.fix: Pods that lie on damp ground or hang through summer rains can grow Aspergillus molds that make aflatoxin, which baking does not destroy; pick dry pods from the tree before the rains.

findings.claim: Freeze picked pods for a few days before milling to kill beetle eggs in the seeds.
findings.because: Pods taken out of the freezer pick up condensation. Pods that are bagged or milled while damp grow the same Aspergillus mold the definition warns about, and the flour's sugar holds that moisture. The step that stops the mold is drying the pods completely after freezing, and it is missing.
findings.fix: Freeze picked pods for a few days to kill beetle eggs in the seeds, then dry them completely before storing or milling: damp pods mold.

findings.claim: Picking pods: dry, straw colored, snapping, sweet when chewed, taken from the tree.
findings.because: The line does not tell a picker to reject pods with dark spots, black or gray fuzz, or a musty smell, which are the visible signs of mold, and it does not give the timing that matters: before the summer rains. It also invites chewing a pod without first confirming the tree. Other desert legumes carry pods too, including Texas mountain laurel, whose seeds are toxic. Mesquite has paired thorns at the nodes and feathery bipinnate leaves.
findings.fix: Picking pods: only from a tree you know as mesquite (paired thorns, feathery leaves), before the summer rains; dry, straw colored, snapping, sweet when chewed. Reject any pod with dark spots, fuzz or a musty smell.

findings.claim: with little starch and no gluten
findings.because: This is true of the pod, but a cook reads 'no gluten' as permission to serve the flour to someone with celiac disease. Small mills often grind or pack it alongside wheat. The house rule says to state the fact about the plant and never imply a verdict about the flour in the bag.
findings.fix: with little starch and no gluten of its own

findings.claim: "grilling", "smoking"
findings.because: These are what a cook does with mesquite WOOD, not with the ingredient this entry covers (the pod flour and syrup). The definition itself says "the flour carries none of it", so the methods list contradicts the entry. "whisking" is also not a method in the corpus vocabulary; the corpus uses "blending" for stirring a powder into a liquid.
findings.fix: ["baking", "toasting", "blending", "simmering", "reducing"]

findings.claim: "The plate files it among fruits, but nobody eats the pod fresh;"
findings.because: Ripe pods are chewed straight off the tree for their sweet pulp, and this entry's own choose field tells the picker to check that the pod is "sweet when chewed". What is true, and what the plate's correction says, is that the pod is not eaten as a fruit is: the fiber and the rock-hard seeds are spat out. This sentence also puts the definition at 997 characters, past the 950 aim, so the replacement should be shorter.
findings.fix: "The plate files it among fruits, but the pod is only ever chewed, not eaten;"

findings.claim: "season": []
findings.because: An empty array claims the item is genuinely year-round, but the entry tells the cook how to pick pods (choose) and how to freeze picked pods (store). Pods ripen only in summer: in the Sonoran and Chihuahuan deserts the main crop comes in June and July, with a smaller late-summer crop in some years. The corpus gives shelf-stable harvested items their harvest months, not an empty array: Almond [8,9,10], Pecan [10,11,12], Date [9,10,11]. As written, a reader can go looking for pods in January.

findings.claim: 'The plate files it among fruits; the pod is a dry one...' is a note to the editor about the category choice, not something a cook needs. A reader who never saw the plate meets an unexplained reference.
findings.because: 'The plate files it among fruits; the pod is a dry one...' is a note to the editor about the category choice, not something a cook needs. A reader who never saw the plate meets an unexplained reference.
findings.fix: Cut 'The plate files it among fruits;' and keep the cook-facing part: 'The pod is dry, chewed off the tree but never served fresh, so a kitchen buys the flour, or a syrup boiled down from soaked pods.'

dispositions.reason: Replaced 'sugar and acid both run high' with 'it also carries more acid on less sugar, so it tastes loud rather than merely sweet'. I kept the direction the finding gives (more acid, less sugar than Evergreen) but dropped 'twice' because I could not confirm the exact ratio myself. The furaneol, linalool and beta-ionone clause is unchanged.
prep now says 'since wet drupelets leak and mold within hours' in place of the dilution reason, which matches the store field and the Blackberry entry.
choose now reads 'a solid block has warmed and refrozen, so expect weeping', which no longer claims the fruit melted.

Replaced 'Cook frozen fruit from frozen.' with the finding's sentence: frozen berries are frozen raw, have carried norovirus and hepatitis A, and freezing does not kill them, so boil them for a minute before any uncooked use and cook them from frozen. It is worded as a fact about the product, not a verdict that a dish is safe. The baking-soda sentence was cut as the finding suggested, so prep is 348 characters, under the 700 ceiling. No banned token ('thaw' included) appears.

The sentence now reads 'which is why over 95 percent of the crop, most of it machine shaken in July, is frozen, pureed or juiced'. The 95 percent figure now goes with processing, softness explains the processing, and machine harvest is 'most' rather than a percentage.

Removed the traits that repeat Blackberry's choose line (dull deep black, plump, no red drupelets, wine smell). choose keeps only what is specific to Marion: its shape, its softness under a fingertip, a stained wet punnet, and the frozen-bag shake, which now carries the fact-3 wording. It is 271 characters.
Removed 'and named for Marion County'. The definition now reads 'released in Oregon in 1956, so', which keeps the cross and the cultivar status the hint requires.
Deleted 'Sieve pulp for sauce or sorbet, where the seeds show.' because it repeats the Blackberry entry. The safety sentence now in prep already names sorbet and fool.
Dropped the unconfirmed sugar comparison; d now reads "milder and less tart than a raspberry", keeping only the acid half, which the sources support.

choose now says "the bush sets the shade, gold to ruby, so match the ripest fruit on that plant". The fruit still changes color as it ripens, so I made the same fix in d: "Color alone is not ripeness ... so judge each plant by its ripest fruit". Otherwise the two fields would disagree.

d now gives the reason: "add pectin, since the fruit has too little to set, rather than boiling it down". That matches the commercial-pectin recipes and sets it apart from Raspberry, which has moderate pectin and sets with lemon and a hard boil.
Qualified to "within hours in a warm bucket", so d no longer contradicts store's one to two days refrigerated.

choose now makes structure the identification check: a ripe berry comes away as a hollow cup of drupelets, never a smooth single berry in a stalked cluster like baneberry or red elderberry. The toxic look-alikes are named as facts about the plants. Also folded in the fact-2 color fix and the defect list. choose is 370 characters, over the 280 target but well under the 700 ceiling, which the contract keeps for look-alike safety text like this.

methods replaced with ["raw","macerating","preserving","freezing","baking"]: method verbs instead of product names, matching Raspberry and the corpus vocabulary, and including freezing, which store recommends.
Lowercased to "built like a raspberry:", which matches the lowercase "raspberry" later in d.
Now "each a thin skin over juicy flesh around one hard pit" and "a separation layer forms between fruit and receptacle", so d uses one name for the structure throughout.

It says a crushed seed yields benzaldehyde, the bitter almond, plus a trace of hydrogen cyanide, and that the leaves and twigs hold more than the fruit. The mg/kg figures are left out: the text cites no sources, and the numbers add nothing a cook uses.
Removed 'cooking brings that almond note forward'. The line now reads 'A baked saskatoon, its seeds softened and split, tastes faintly of marzipan', so it no longer says heat creates the compound.
Removed 'lemon juice fixes both'. The definition now says 'Pectin is low too, so a jam wants added pectin or a long reduction', which agrees with Huckleberry.

The definition now gives the pH as about 4.2 to 4.4, just under the 4.6 line for water-bath canning, and says a jar takes bottled lemon juice, about 15 grams per pint, as acid rather than seasoning. Lemon still lifts a flat filling.
Replaced the repeated anthocyanin and green-gray explanation with a cross-reference: 'The pigment answers to pH as in Blueberry, so keep baking soda modest.'

The opening now reads 'the saskatoon is A. alnifolia, and juneberry or shadbush usually an eastern cousin such as A. canadensis'. 'Usually' stays because in the Dakotas 'juneberry' is also used for A. alnifolia.
In choose, 'moldy berries' is now 'moldy fruit'.
Same change as fact-4. The definition states the pH range, how close it sits to the 4.6 water-bath line, and that lemon juice in a jar is part of the acid, not seasoning.

Added the identification check to choose. Every fruit has a five-pointed dried crown and several soft seeds; blue-black fruit with no crown and three or four hard seeds, packed at the leaf bases, is buckthorn, a strong purgative. The mountain ash sentence keeps the plate correction's hedged wording ('belongs to another tree, such as'). Choose is now 485 characters, under the 700 ceiling that safety content is allowed.

Prep now says to pick off every stem and leaf 'which hold more glycoside than the fruit', and the definition names the glycoside. The claim that underripe fruit carries more was left out because I could not confirm it.

The definition now states the toxin plainly: amygdalin, a cyanogenic glycoside that yields hydrogen cyanide from a crushed seed. It no longer suggests heat increases it. I left out the finding's claim that the glycosides fall during cooking, and the mg/kg figures, because I could not confirm them; the rules say to omit what is uncertain.

Covered by the fact-3 and fact-4 changes: the pH against the 4.6 line, lemon in the jar as acid, and low pectin needing added pectin or a long reduction. The pH is given as the range 4.2 to 4.4, not a single 4.4.

Used the proposed prep field almost word for word: 'Pick off every stem and leaf, which hold more glycoside than the fruit; rinse just before use and towel dry...' It is 271 characters, inside the 280 limit.
The sentence now cross-references Blueberry ('The pigment answers to pH as in Blueberry'), so it no longer repeats Blueberry's content, and the unhyphenated 'green gray' is gone.
Same change as fact-7: 'Reject split, leaking or moldy fruit: one wet one spoils the basket.'

The definition now gives the reason as a fact about the plant. The seeds are tiny and each holds only a trace, which is why they stay in the way apple pips do in an apple eaten whole. The benzaldehyde and hydrogen cyanide aside is cut to one clause, and the apricot-kernel comparison is gone. I also dropped 'softened and split' from the baked-fruit line, because it implied crushing the seeds. Prep now says the seeds stay in whole and that a smooth sauce goes through a food mill, not a blender. That keeps the no-grinding rule in Loquat, Hawthorn, Crabapple and Quince. The definition is 1010 characters, prep 328, and no banned tokens or dashes.

Replaced 'Pectin and acid together are why haws set a firm jelly with no added pectin' with 'Haws carry ample pectin but hedgerow fruit is short of acid, so jelly takes lemon and no added pectin.' This matches the entry's own 'only mildly tart raw' line and the standard haw jelly method.

Changed to 'kin to apple and quince but built, like medlar, the other way round'. Medlar also carries bony pyrenes and is the sister genus, so it belongs on hawthorn's side of the comparison, not the apple's.

The method now reads 'Simmer them whole until soft, about 45 minutes, then drip the liquor through a jelly bag for jelly or food-mill it for haw cheese'. The split skin is gone as the cue, and jelly liquor is kept apart from milled pulp.
Merged with safety-6 and contract-10. The choose line now names firethorn (thorny but evergreen with small unlobed leaves) and says cotoneaster is thornless, so thorns alone no longer pass the test.
Choose now opens 'Deep red, or black on black hawthorn'. C. douglasii, the native Northwest species on the plate, ripens purple-black.

The check is now 'a deciduous tree with thorns, its leaves usually lobed', with firethorn told apart as evergreen and unlobed. I used 'usually lobed' rather than a flat rule because some Crataegus, such as cockspur hawthorn, have unlobed leaves. Deciduous plus thorns is the reliable split from firethorn. The hazard is now stated as a fact about the plants: both look-alike fruits upset the stomach raw.

Store now says dried shanzha slices 'many still hold stones: pick them out before grinding or blending, or steep and strain.' I said 'hold stones' rather than 'cut stone pieces' because some commercial slices are seeded and I could not confirm that the stones are routinely cut.

Added after the shanzha sentence: 'Concentrated hawthorn, as strong tea or extract, can add to the action of digoxin and blood pressure drugs.' It is stated as a fact about the plant, with no verdict on any dish. The definition stays at 1100 characters, inside 1200.

Applied together with fact-1 and fact-3. Lemon supplies the acid, no added pectin is needed, and the juice is dripped through a jelly bag for jelly, while milled pulp goes to haw cheese. The tanghulu clause is kept.

Applied with fact-4 and safety-6, and the choose field was tightened ('stalks on', 'shanzha large, bright red and freckled pale'). It comes to 363 characters: above the 280 aim but well under the 700 ceiling, which the contract keeps for look-alike warnings like this one.
Replaced 'since cooking undoes any softening' with 'which never needs their texture'. Freezing ruptures the cells for good, and jelly never uses the fruit's texture anyway.

The amygdalin sentence is cut from the definition and now appears once, in prep, in the critic's wording and credited to crabapple. The grind-or-blend warning is gone from store. The dried-shanzha note stays there as a use note: steep or simmer, then strain. The second pectin line is now only about acid: 'Hedgerow fruit is short of acid, so jelly takes lemon and needs no added pectin.' I also changed 'Simmer them' to 'Simmer haws', because the sentence that used to come before it had changed. Lengths: definition 958, prep 279. No banned tokens and no dashes.

'No starch' is now 'almost no starch', which matches the Apricot and Raspberry entries. The sentence is also rebuilt so the missing starch leads to 'must come off fully ripe', that leads to 'ripe it lasts two days', and the two-day life is what keeps it out of shops. I used 'rarely sold fresh' instead of 'keeps it out of shops' because fresh boysenberries do still sell at farm stands.

Prep now opens 'Wash only if you must, just before use', which matches Raspberry ('Do not wash unless you must') and Blackberry ('Shop fruit needs nothing'). I did not take this finding's 'bowl, never the tap' method. It conflicts with boysenberry-safety-4 and with the FDA's running-water guidance, so the gentle colander stream from that finding is used instead.

Store now says frozen berries have carried hepatitis A and norovirus, that freezing does not kill either virus, and that the berries should be boiled for a minute in sauce, jam or a bubbling pie rather than served raw. This follows the FSAI advice to boil for one minute. It is written as a fact about the product, not a verdict that a dish is safe. 'Never for garnish' is gone because the texture point is already in the definition. The field is now about 350 characters, above the 280 aim but well under the 700 ceiling, which the contract keeps for safety text like this. It uses no banned words.

The bowl soak is now 'set them in a colander under a gentle stream of cold water, then spread them on a towel'. That is the FDA's running-water guidance, and it stops one moldy berry from spreading spores through shared water. It fits inside the 'wash only if you must' opening from boysenberry-fact-2. Prep is 278 characters.

The definition now opens on the mechanism: large, thin-skinned, juicy drupelets on a soft core that come off the cane with the fruit and tear under their own weight. The 1920s California cross of blackberry, raspberry and loganberry comes after the mechanism, trimmed to one clause. It still agrees with the plate correction that the fruit's home is California.

The cause now comes first and the conclusion last, as this finding proposed: almost no starch, so it must be picked ripe, and ripe it lasts two days. 'That fragility' became 'that short life' so the closing clause points at the two days just named. 'No starch' was softened to 'almost no starch' to satisfy boysenberry-fact-1.

I cut the cyanidin, pH and baking-soda sentence and put the Serviceberry-style cross-reference in its place: 'its pigment answers to pH as in Blueberry'. I also dropped the frozen-slump, extra-starch close and left the frozen-pie instruction to Marionberry. The new close is about what only this berry has. Its raspberry ancestry gives it a winey, floral perfume, and its seeds are large and hard, so a sieved puree is its natural form. The definition now ends on a concrete next step: collapse the fruit with sugar and lemon, sieve it, and build syrup, sorbet, coulis or smooth jam from what comes through. That also contrasts cleanly with Marionberry, whose smaller seeds let it skip the sieve. The definition is 903 characters.

I moved the hepatitis A and norovirus fact out of store and into prep, in Marionberry's wording: a full one-minute boil before the berries go into anything served uncooked, and cook them from frozen. Store is now about storage only. While there, I changed the rinse instruction to match Marionberry and Black Raspberry (a bowl of cold water, not under the tap), because a colander under the tap contradicted both siblings. I also added 'pieces' of care to store: pick out any leaker on arrival. Prep is 330 characters, over the 280 target but well under the 700 ceiling, because the safety sentence needs its full wording. Methods: I added 'pureeing' to match the new close.
Removed 'bakes as well as fresh'. Store now says frozen fruit sieves as well as fresh and should be baked still frozen, because once it softens it bleeds pigment and juice into the batter.
Changed 'slipping off the stem' to 'slips off its white core at a touch'. The test is now tied to picking ('on the cane'), which matches the receptacle distinction in the definition.

Added a wild-picking sentence: take only hollow caps of drupelets off a thorny cane with a white bloom; a smooth, glossy single berry belongs to a poisonous plant such as pokeweed or nightshade (see Blackberry). I wrote 'belongs to a poisonous plant' so the claim is a fact about the plant. Choose is now 468 characters. That is under the 700 ceiling, which the contract keeps for look-alike warnings.

Prep now reads 'Pick over on a tray. Rinse wild fruit just before use: dip it briefly in a bowl of cold water and drain on paper.' Rinsing wild fruit is now the default, as in the Blackberry entry. Store still says unwashed.
Lowercased 'raspberry' and 'blackberry' in the first sentence of the definition. They now match the corpus and the entry's own 'red raspberry'.
Rewrote store with the house temperature form '0 to 2 C (32 to 36 F)'. The dangling 'it' is gone: 'mold spreads berry to berry, so lift out soft ones'.
Store now says 'frozen fruit slumps but keeps its flavor', which agrees with Blackberry ('the texture goes but the flavor holds'). The overstated 'bakes as well as fresh' is gone.

Used the proposed wording for the first sentence ('Dull black all over, plump and dry; on the cane a ripe one slips off its ... core at a touch') and dropped the repeated 'hollow inside'. I kept 'white' before core so the term matches the definition. The safety finding's look-alike sentence then took the field past 280, which the contract allows for that warning.

dispositions.finding: black-raspberry-critic-1 (1): the pH paragraph repeats Blueberry, Huckleberry and Boysenberry
dispositions.reason: The cyanidin rutinoside fact stays. The pH clause is now 'and like Blueberry it turns blue-green against baking soda', so the entry points to the sibling that explains pH instead of repeating it.

dispositions.finding: black-raspberry-critic-1 (2): the cross-reference sends pokeweed to Blackberry, which never names it
dispositions.reason: Changed to '(see Blackberry and Elderberry)'. Elderberry covers pokeweed and Blackberry covers nightshade, so each look-alike named now has an entry that treats it.

dispositions.finding: black-raspberry-critic-1 (3): the frozen-berry hepatitis A and norovirus fact is missing, and the sauce is only warmed
dispositions.reason: The definition now says most of the commercial crop is sold frozen. Prep states the hazard as a fact about the fruit: freezing keeps hepatitis A and norovirus alive and both have ridden frozen berries, so bought frozen fruit for anything served uncooked gets a full minute at the boil. The sauce step now says boil rather than warm. It is not a verdict on any dish. Prep runs 432 characters, above the 280 aim but under the 700 ceiling, the room the contract keeps for a safety fact.

The closing line of d now reads: crush whole berries without cracking the seeds and heat them for juice and jelly, since the hull holds the color; split pulp from hull for hull pie. The words 'without cracking the seeds' keep it consistent with the prep warning about bitter seed tannin. Prep now opens with 'For hull pie,' so the squeeze-out method is tied to the dish it belongs to.
d now says the hull is rich in ellagic acid and ellagitannins, which settle out of the juice as sediment. The claim that the sediment is the same compound is gone.
'a few to a loose cluster' is now 'in small loose clusters'. This is merged with the contract-9 rewrite of the same clause.
'Inside is a slipskin gel around' is now 'Inside, a gel pulp that slips free of the hull holds'.
In prep, 'until the seeds float free' is now 'until the seeds come loose'.

The choose color test now reads: bronze gone golden or dark types gone evenly purple-black with no red cast. 'With slight give' was added. The line rejecting bronze fruit that is still green was dropped, because ripe bronze fruit can stay greenish. 'Rock-hard' was added to the reject list. The 'leaks and molds' wording was cut to 'molds'.

Added the proposed sentence on moonseed nearly word for word at the end of choose: judge the seed's shape, not the count; grape seeds are plump teardrops, and moonseed has smooth-edged leaves, no tendrils and one flat crescent-shaped seed. It is stated as a fact about the plant, not as a verdict that the fruit is safe. choose is now 501 characters, under the 700 ceiling.

The wording that ends ripening at deep purple is gone. Dark types now pass only when they are 'evenly purple-black with no red cast', so fruit that still shows red or purple-red is rejected. This wording answers both contract-8 and fact-6, which proposed purple-black.

Cut the chromosome count. The opening clause now reads 'its berries grow in small loose clusters, ripen one at a time and drop when ready', which fixes the agreement problem where the cluster seemed to ripen.
In methods, 'jelly' is replaced with 'fermenting', which covers the sweet wine named in the hint. Jelly is still covered by 'preserving'.

Added the airway fact to prep, where the squeeze technique lives, worded as a fact about the fruit (the slipped pulp is a slippery, grape-sized ball that can block a small airway), followed by the fix of splitting it and removing the seeds for a child under five. This matches the Table Grape entry's guidance without repeating it. Prep is now 436 characters, under the 700 ceiling, and uses no dashes or banned words. No other field changed.
Seed count changed from 'two to four' to 'usually three to five', which matches Morton (1 to 10 seeds, usually 3 to 5). The hint's figure was wrong.
Store now reads 'two or three days on the counter and about a week refrigerated at 2 to 4 C (36 to 39 F)'. I used the true Fahrenheit conversion (39 F, not 40 F), which also answers contract-10.
Changed 'weeks ahead of any stone fruit' to 'one of the first tree fruits of the year'. Loquat and cherry seasons overlap in California and Spain, so the old absolute claim was false.
Changed 'It does not ripen off the tree' to 'It will not sweeten off the tree'. Color and acid shift a little after picking but sugar does not rise, and sugar is the fact the cook needs.

Prep now ends 'Discard the seeds whole: never grind, crush or steep them.' That names how people actually get poisoned: liqueur, seed powder and seeds simmered in jam. I cut 'with your fingers', 'from the stem end' and 'that lines their cavity' so the field stays at 269 characters, even with the calyx step from contract-12.
The definition now says the amygdalin is what 'the seed's own enzyme turns into hydrogen cyanide once it is crushed or chewed'. That states the mechanism and covers chewing as well as crushing.

Added the sentence 'Its allergy proteins are close kin to those in peach and apple, and people allergic to those fruits have reacted to loquat.' just before the closing line. It states a fact about the fruit, not a verdict. To keep the definition under the 1200 ceiling (it is about 985 characters now), I tightened the polyphenol oxidase sentence and the pectin sentence without losing either fact.
Changed 'harmless' to 'cosmetic', which is a word about quality and not a safety verdict.
Changed the wording to 'so never pile them, and wash them only as you use them', which gives each instruction its own verb.
The store temperature now uses the true conversion, as part of the fact-2 range: '2 to 4 C (36 to 39 F)'. This matches the Apricot entry. 40 F appears nowhere.

Replaced the repeated 'a green one will never sweeten' with 'fruit sold with a bit of stem still on keeps better than bare fruit'. Loquats are clipped with the stem on because pulling them tears the skin at the top. The green-shoulder fact is still stated once in choose and once in d.
Prep now opens 'Pull the stem, nick off the dry calyx at the blossom end, and slip the skin off'. That covers the part people get wrong: the persistent dry calyx tuft is gritty and has to be cut off.
The closing line now reads 'Eat the softest raw the day you get them', so it no longer contradicts the week of refrigerated storage given for ripe fruit.
Replaced 'chutney', which is a dish, with 'pickling'. Pickling is the corpus method term for vinegar-spiced loquat preserves, and every method is now a gerund or 'raw'.

The definition now opens on the mechanism the critic named: a rose-family pome whose sugar is set at picking, so it will not sweeten off the tree and a green shoulder stays sour. The botany and calendar opening is gone. The flowering calendar is left to the season field, and spring comes back only as a short clause tied to the browning mechanism ('the first tree fruit of spring travels so badly'). I also changed the seed count from 'usually three to five' to 'one to five of them'. That range is safe to state, and it does not conflict with the hint's 'two to four'. The definition went from about 1050 to 887 characters, which is inside the 650 to 950 target. The other fields are unchanged.

The definition now says that outside the South the name means the dried Pisum pea, sold whole or split. This is merged with contract-6 into one clause: 'elsewhere the name means the dried Pisum pea, whole or split.'
Changed to 'Calcium cross-links the pectin that glues the cells together and acid slows its breakdown'. The conclusion that hard water or an early tomato stalls the peas is unchanged.

The store field now reads 'Dried keep a year sealed; pinholes mean weevil, and older seed hardens and may never soften.' That names the weevil sign and states the hard-to-cook defect, and the field stays at 280 characters.

Removed the buying advice and added 'Raw peas carry lectins and trypsin inhibitors: cook through before dressing a salad.' It is stated as a fact about the seed, with no hard-boil warning, which agrees with the Black-eyed Pea entry. Marinating stays in methods, and prep is 278 characters.

The definition now opens on the mechanism: 'The seed coat decides the pot...'. The separate 'The difference in the pot is the seed coat' sentence is gone, and the dried-versus-fresh timing sentence is tightened. The definition went from 965 to 975 characters even with the new Pisum clause, and the crowder, cream and purple hull clauses are unchanged.
Merged with fact-1: 'elsewhere the name means the dried Pisum pea, whole or split' now sits right after the Southern usage.
Answered by the same edit as fact-2. It uses fact-2's more exact wording, where calcium cross-links and acid slows breakdown, instead of treating the two as one mechanism.
The gap between one and two years is gone. The field now says that older seed hardens and may never soften, merged with fact-3.
Removed 'buy them shelled when you can'. The pick-over sentence now drops 'the shriveled, split and weevil-holed', as this finding proposed.
Removed 'braising'. Methods are now simmering, stewing, blanching, marinating and frying.

Store now says cook within 2 days, which matches Black-eyed Pea (280 chars, still inside the ceiling). The Pisum clause is cut down to 'not the dried Pisum field pea of split-pea soup', so the entry plainly covers the Southern cowpea only and a split-pea reader is told to look elsewhere. The definition is now 962 characters. Season stays June to September, in line with the plate correction.

Removed the 15 minute parboil. Prep now says to boil uncovered in plenty of fresh water until tender, dried ones for at least 30 minutes, and to drain before finishing with the hock. It covers fresh as well as dried beans. The 8 to 12 hour soak stays because the finding's own fix keeps it, and the long boil does the leaching.

Dropped the flat-versus-plump tell, which was backwards. Dried lima is now 'flat, smooth, cream or pale green half-moons, a white eye midway along the inner curve'. The fava tell is now 'a tan to brown bean with a long black scar at one end'. That agrees with the eye position and color, and it leaves out thickness, which varies between fava types.

Opening is now 'one species under many names: baby lima, Fordhook and butter bean, which in the South means the fresh ones, often small, and in Britain the large dried cream ones'. That matches the Southeastern Vegetables plate, which prints Butter Beans / Lima Beans.
The mechanism now has both steps: linamarase 'splits it to a cyanohydrin that falls apart into hydrogen cyanide'. I kept it mechanism-first rather than using the vaguer 'starts it breaking down'.
Now reads 'heat kills the enzyme and leaves linamarin that gut bacteria can still split'.
Store now reads 'warmth and damp, far more than age, cause the hard-to-cook defect'.
Prep now says of fresh beans 'never eat them raw', and the boil-and-drain step covers fresh beans explicitly.

Same fix as fact-1. The 15 minute figure is gone. Beans boil uncovered in fresh water until tender (dried at least 30 minutes) and are drained, and only then go in with the hock, so the leaching water is never the liquid people eat.
Same change as fact-5: leftover linamarin is now said to be split by gut bacteria, which is why the water steps are needed.

Now reads 'Bred cream and green types are low in it; wild-type black or purple seeds run many times higher, so pass them by, and keep the soak and boil either way.' I wrote 'wild-type black or purple' rather than 'dark' so the line does not turn cooks away from speckled Southern butter beans or Christmas limas, which are bred commercial types.
Choose now names vicine and convicine and says they bring on favism 'cooked or not'. This agrees with the Fava Bean entry, which says cooking does not destroy them.

Prep now covers fresh and dried: boil uncovered in plenty of fresh water until tender (dried at least 30 minutes), drain, then finish with the simmered ham hock. This matches the definition's 'drained off too'.
Now reads 'simmer the ham hock from the start in its own pot, add the drained beans, and the corn only for the last five minutes', so the hock never sits in the bean water.
Now reads 'Water is what works: linamarin and cyanide both dissolve'. The pair is named at once, and I avoided repeating 'the fix' from the sentence before.
Merged with fact-3. In the South 'butter bean' now means the fresh ones, often small, and in Britain the large dried cream ones, which matches the plate.

Dried now names the defect to reject ('reject cracked or pinholed'). The fava line is rewritten with the corrected tell from fact-2, not the 'flatter, thick-skinned' wording this fix proposed. The field is 382 characters: over the 280 aim but well under the 700 ceiling, which the contract keeps for safety look-alikes like this one.
Now reads 'Shell fresh ones by snipping or tearing open the tough curved seam'. Lima pods are leathery and a thumb often will not open them.

The phrase 'dark seeded types' was rewritten under safety-10 as 'wild-type black or purple seeds'. The one compound modifier left is hyphenated and nothing stays unhyphenated. No em or spaced en dash was added.
Store now reads 'spread in one layer and cold within 2 hours of the roaster', which matches the Hatch Chile store field word for word on timing. 'The same day' is gone.

The Hatch entry calls Hatch earthy and the plate correction calls Pueblo earthy, so earth cannot be the contrast. The closing contrast now reads 'the honest answer: more wall and more heat, the same roasted earth.'
Now reads 'the pods set pointing up off the plant, drooping only when full and heavy'.

Replaced with 'MOSCO is the best-known cultivar, a Colorado State selection from one family's Arkansas Valley seed line.' It no longer says Mosco is the only Pueblo chile or that it is simply a family line.
Store now reads 'Fresh, a week in the crisper, dry, in a paper or perforated bag.' The pod no longer sits loose and drying out.

Prep now opens 'Peel only what you will cook: freshly roasted pods after 10 minutes sweating in a covered bowl, frozen ones as they soften', which agrees with store and with Hatch. The banned token 'thaw' is avoided.
'September drum roasters' is now 'late-summer drum roasters', which fits the August to October season.

Used this fix for store, since it is the most complete version of the same finding: one layer, cold within 2 hours of the roaster, then 3 days refrigerated or a year frozen with the skins on. That restores Hatch's refrigerated option.

The oil sentence now reads 'Roasted chile under oil lives in the fridge and is used within 4 days, or frozen: low acid and airless is where botulism grows.' That is the standard guidance for low-acid vegetables in oil, and it no longer implies that indefinite storage in the fridge is safe.
Prep adds 'Char under a running hood: the smoke carries capsaicin.' and 'keep hands off eyes until washed'. The gloves note stays.
This is the same defect as fact-1 and safety-8, and it is answered by the same store rewrite: cold within 2 hours, skins on, a year frozen, citing Hatch correctly.
'thick and meaty' is now 'thicker and meatier', a difference of degree, so it no longer implies that Hatch (which its entry calls thick-walled) is thin.

Answered with the fact-2 wording, 'more wall and more heat, the same roasted earth'. The Hatch entry credits Hatch with sugar, but fact-2 notes that sellers also call Mosco sweet, so the claim sweetness makes is left out and both chiles keep their earth.
Heat now reads 'roughly 5,000 to 20,000 Scoville, well above a Big Jim Hatch'. This is the range the plate correction gives, and it can be checked against Hatch's 500 to 2,500 for Big Jim.

The definition now opens on the mechanism: the thicker wall that takes the char, lets steam lift the skin and holds shape in a stew, then the heat mechanism. Etymology and provenance move to the middle and are shortened. d is 993 characters.
Removed 'taste a strip first' from prep, since the definition already closes on it. Added 'Keep the juice that pools under the pods', which agrees with the Hatch prep.
Removed 'peeling' from methods. It is a prep step and is covered in prep.
d now reads "a dense mesh of hyphae whose basidia will bear spores"; the basidia bear the spores and the hyphae remain as capillitium.

d now reads "Any tint at all, yellow, olive or purple, means past." This covers the purple-spored C. cyathiformis, which never turns yellow.

This one change also answers contract-14.
choose now calls the earthball poisonous and adds the purple-black marbling as a second sign. The rind wording was merged with safety-10.

choose now says liver damage shows from day two to four and can end in liver failure within the week, so it no longer implies the danger is over after day four. The sentence was merged with safety-11.

This sentence was added to d after the gilled-button sentence: "A hard rind millimeters thick on the cut face, around a firm interior, means an earthball." A reader of the definition alone now has the earthball check too.
choose now opens "Firm but springy like marshmallow, never hard or rigid". The words "Heavy, firm" are gone, because that is how an earthball feels.

choose now describes the rind for the whole genus: "thick, hard rind, a distinct band on the cut face, yellowish to brown and scaly or cracked, around a firm interior that soon marbles purple-black". A brown S. areolatum, S. verrucosum or S. cepa is no longer passed over.

choose now says the easing is not recovery and closes with "Keep one raw specimen back from every batch." The timeline wording follows fact-7. The field is 662 characters, under the 700 ceiling, and the overage is look-alike and poisoning material.
store now says to discard the puffball if any face has tinted, rather than trimming the yellow part. This agrees with d's verdict on the whole specimen, and "tinted" follows fact-4.
store now opens "Halved for the check, in a paper bag..." and says "cut a fresh face before cooking". It no longer contradicts the halve-every-specimen test.
This is the same fix as fact-5: the gilled-button sentence no longer says "means a young Amanita button". It now reads "a gilled mushroom's button, possibly a death cap or destroying angel".

The repetition was removed. choose no longer restates d's white-face and outline test ("each face pure white and uniform, no cap, gill or stem outline") or says "mushroomy".
